articles.title: How hawkmoths turned their genitals into bat-busting weapons
articles.author: Elie Dolgin

paras.en: When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.

But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.
The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.

“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.

The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.

The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.

Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.

These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.

Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”

The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.

But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.
“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”

articles.title: Moths Keep Evolving Their Genitals Into Anti-Bat Weapons, Again And Again
articles.author: Michelle Starr

paras.en: Some evolutionary innovations are so useful that nature keeps on making them.

There's the crab; everyone knows nature keeps making crabs. There's the ability to fly, whether by feathers, membranes, or chitin. And, of course, there's the indispensable trick of using one's genitals to scramble the sonar of hunting bats.
No, your eyes are not deceiving you. Some moths have evolved the ability to make noise at bats using their genital structures.
And apparently it's so useful that this ability has emerged, separately, again and again in different species of hawkmoths.

According to new research, these moths have evolved the ability to scream at bats using their genitals independently as many as seven times over 30 million years – and at least three distinct anatomical mechanisms have emerged, producing different kinds of potentially sonar-jamming ultrasound.

"Collectively," writes the team in a study led by entomologist Paul Masonick of the Florida Museum of Natural History, "our findings deepen our understanding of defensive bioacoustic adaptations in this iconic predator-prey system."

The relationship between predator and prey is one of nature's most powerful drivers of evolution. The constant threat of death from a particular source – a predator on the prowl for snacks – creates pressure to find ways to avoid ending up on the menu.

We see it time and again – an evolutionary arms race in which predators and prey continually evolve new ways to outwit each other, driving adaptations such as camouflage, toxicity, spikes, armor, and ways to look much bigger and tougher than the reality might be.
For hawkmoths harried by hungry bats, producing sounds that confuse the echolocation their predators use to locate flying prey in the darkness has the potential to be a powerful survival strategy.
But moths don't have larynxes. So they have to get a little bit more creative.

The trick is a process called stridulation – producing sound by rubbing two body parts together, like the chirps of crickets rubbing their wings, or the hissing of spiders rubbing their legs against each other.

In male hawkmoths, the instruments are specialized scales on a pair of genital structures called valvae. By moving these structures against modified surfaces on their abdomens, the moths can produce bursts of ultrasound.
And, as the researchers discovered, there is more than one way to make genital music.
Masonick and his colleagues examined the genital structures of male hawkmoths from across the family, using detailed imaging to identify the surfaces responsible for producing their ultrasonic calls.

In some species, specialized scales on the genital structures scrape against other scales on the abdomen. In others, they rub against tiny spines. And in a third group, the scales scrape across little bumps called nodules.

Each mechanism produces its own distinctive ultrasonic sounds – a tiny percussion band that's beyond the range of human hearing – but when slowed down to bring them into the audible range, they resemble a series of rapid clicks, buzzes, or trills.
The scale-on-scale mechanism tends to produce shorter, more intermittent bursts of ultrasound, while scale-on-spine moths produce longer, more sustained emissions.
The scale-on-nodule moths, meanwhile, seem to have the most varied repertoire, producing sounds that differ considerably even between closely related species.
And, amazingly, these three distinct mechanisms for yelling from the gonads weren't all inherited from a single, acoustically gifted ancestor.

When the researchers mapped the sound-producing structures and behaviors onto the hawkmoth family tree, they found that the ability to sing an ultrasonic genital song in response to hunting bats appears to have repeatedly evolved independently, as many as seven times over the past 30 million years.
Which raises the question: If nature kept reinventing the screaming willy, just how useful is it?
Surprisingly, the answer is: not consistently – at least, maybe not in the way you might expect.
The researchers analyzed recordings of the moths' ultrasonic performances, measuring how long each burst lasted, its frequency, and how much time the moths spent making noise.
They then compared these measurements with what previous experiments had revealed about the kinds of sounds that can interfere with bat echolocation.
And not all the strange moth songs were up to the task.
The more sustained sounds were most likely to have the acoustic characteristics associated with disrupting bat sonar in a way that could help the moth evade a toothy capture.
But even the shorter bursts may have their uses.

Some hawkmoths have hearing organs that allow them to detect the ultrasonic calls of approaching bats, giving them time to respond with a barrage of noise. That's when it would be useful to mess with echolocation.
Others, however, are deaf. They can't hear the bats coming, so they can't respond to approaching predators in the same way. However, they can still produce ultrasound when touched.

The researchers suggest that shorter bursts might startle a bat as it closes in for the kill, potentially giving the moth a chance to escape. Well, and it would, wouldn't it? Imagine going in for a tasty snack, and its genitals start yelling at you. You'd back right the hell off.

Another possibility is acoustic mimicry. Some moths use ultrasonic signals to warn bats that they're toxic or otherwise unpleasant to eat. Hawkmoths, which are generally palatable to bats, may be jumping on the warning bandwagon by making similar sounds.
And there might be another, more appropriate use for the genital sounds, at least in some species.
The variety of sounds produced by the scale-on-nodule mechanism raises the possibility that the sounds could also help moths recognize members of their own species during courtship.
This remains to be tested, but nature is very good at finding new uses for old tricks.
So there you have it – if you can't avoid turning into dinner, maybe at least you can get a little romance before you go.
The research has been published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences.

articles.title: Medieval Humans Partly Caused Two Catastrophic Lake Tsunamis, And We Could Easily Do It Again, Scientists Warn
articles.author: Jess Cockerill

paras.en: Tsunamis are not exclusive to the ocean: with the right conditions, they can happen in lakes, too.
At Lake Iseo in northern Italy, medieval humans set the scene for two such catastrophic wave events, and researchers are warning that it could easily happen again.

In a paper published in Nature Communications, an international team has brought together data from sediment cores, seismic profiles, a medieval manuscript, archaeological records, and the modern-day lake itself.
This range of sources helped them recreate the unusual medieval disasters via computer models.

Lake Iseo is downstream of the Italian Alps, from which it receives a regular supply of water via snowmelt. The same tectonic activity that helped to form the Alps also brings the occasional earthquake to the region.
Two thousand years of intensifying land use changed the way sediment settled in the delta, making its sides steeper.

Before the Middle Ages, the Oglio River delta was surrounded by forest. When it rained, loose sediment would flow downhill, but its passage was slowed by the dense networks of tree roots and fungi that held the soil together.
Underwater, the delta's slopes were gentle, gradually tilting towards the lake's deepest point, which is around 250 meters.
But things rapidly changed around the fall of the Roman Empire.

In the centuries that followed, more and more forests that once surrounded the delta were removed for pasture and mining; the human population grew; and three times more sediment was flushed into the lake each year on average.
More and more sediment accumulated at the lake's northern end, creating precariously steep underwater banks just waiting to crash.
And that's exactly what happened, twice.
The natural shape of the delta could handle some seismic activity from time to time without necessarily flooding the surrounding towns.

But when the violent 1117 CE Verona Earthquake shook the lake's steepened banks, they collapsed in an underwater landslide, displacing a massive amount of water that, according to the researchers' modeling, would have flooded large sections of the shores of Lake Iseo without a minute's warning.

"Our simulations reveal that the medieval delta collapses in Lake Iseo generated some of the largest subaquatic landslide-induced tsunamis ever inferred in a lacustrine setting," the study's authors write.
By their calculations, waves in the northern part of the lake would have exceeded 50 meters, inundating nearby shores in less than a minute, with water reaching up to 2.7 kilometers inland.
A 12th-century manuscript now held at the Vatican Library describes the catastrophic event in vivid detail that matches the modeling well. The passage is translated to English as follows:

"The lake overflowed so much that very few of the inhabitants of the nearby villages escaped this danger. Many castles and fortresses also collapsed miserably, with the destruction of their inhabitants."

But alas, medieval folks are not especially known for their scientific inquiry – disasters like this were more likely seen as a message from God. They rebuilt, and resumed the practices that had led to the first fatal tsunami.
Just over a century later, a second earthquake hit: the 1222 CE Brescia earthquake.
Another large tsunami ensued in Lake Iseo, with waves peaking at around 13 meters, and water rushing up to 1 kilometer inland.

"Both tsunamis propagated rapidly across Lake Iseo and were strongly influenced by Monte Isola, the central island, which acts as a natural barrier, splitting the waves and partially shielding the cities behind it," the authors explain.

"Despite this protection, areas such as [the town of] Iseo still experienced significant impacts, with maximum wave heights of ~5.5 meters (1117 CE) and ~2 meters (1222 CE), arriving ~7 minutes after the landslides."
Lake Iseo now has the most densely built shores of any lake in the Italian Alps. Meanwhile, more than eight centuries' worth of sediment has built up since the 1222 CE collapse.

"A tsunami comparable in magnitude to the catastrophic events that struck Lake Iseo during the medieval period would cause severe devastation today, given the region's dense population and shoreline development," the authors write.

"A global lake synthesis showed that human-driven erosion has reached its highest levels since the Industrial Era, progressively overloading deltas worldwide; thus, similar catastrophic failures may become more likely in the future."
The research has been published in Nature Communications.

articles.title: Almost 75% of Deceased NFL Players Had Degenerative Brain Disease, Major Study Estimates
articles.author: Peter Dockrill

paras.en: In 2017, a bombshell discovery rocked the world of American football.

Alarmingly, scientists found that 99 percent of examined brains from deceased NFL players bore signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative neurological condition linked with repeated blows to the head.
In the years since, studies have revealed numerous sports increase the risk of brain injuries from repetitive head trauma, including soccer and rugby.

In the case of CTE among former NFL players, though, it's been difficult to identify just how common the brain disease is, but a new study appears to give us the most accurate assessment yet, suggesting about three-quarters of professional players had the condition when they died.
"Current knowledge regarding CTE neuropathology in American football players is derived from autopsy-based studies," researchers report in a new paper published in JAMA Network Open.
"Autopsy studies are inherently susceptible to registry bias, which may distort estimates of both disease prevalence and associations of exposures with outcomes."
In other words, when scientists study the post-mortem brains of ex-NFL players that have been donated to science, their results are limited to those specific donations.
For example, the landmark 2017 study found signs of CTE in 110 out of 111 (99 percent) of brains studied – but that doesn't mean that 99 percent of all NFL players would develop the disease.

That's because players who experience cognitive, mood, or behavioral symptoms would be expected to be more likely to participate in brain donation, resulting in a form of selection bias (aka 'registry' bias in this context).
In August this year, researchers published a study that took some preliminary steps to account for that bias, identifying all 1,712 former NFL players who died during the years 2008–2021.
Of that group, 338 had donated their brains for study, and 315 of them had a diagnosis of CTE.

But because most of the former deceased players had not donated their brains for study, all researchers could conclude was that CTE prevalence at death ranged somewhere between 18.5 percent and 98.7 percent – or between 24.5 percent and 97.7 percent for players who died between 2016 and 2021.

In the new study, several members of the same research team refined these estimate ranges by combining data from the UNITE brain bank with population-level mortality records for all deceased NFL players identified through the National Death Index (NDI).

After modeling the selection bias effect – estimating that players with cognitive symptoms were approximately five times more likely to have their brains donated for study – the researchers calculated what they claim is the first estimate of population-level prevalence of CTE neuropathology among former NFL players at the time of their death.
It's a breakthrough. But for the NFL community, it's an undeniably grim statistic.

"After adjusting for this selection process, we estimated that approximately 74.5 percent of deceased former NFL players had CTE neuropathology at death between 2008 and 2023," the team explains in their study, led by biostatistician Julia Gallini from Boston University.

While the findings are certainly concerning, they don't mean that three-quarters of former NFL players are destined to develop dementia, says study co-author and neuroscientist Daniel Daneshvar from Harvard Medical School.

"In our clinic with former players, particularly those in midlife, we have had success improving cognitive symptoms, mental health and quality of life through both targeted treatments and proactive brain health strategies," Daneshvar explains.
"While we cannot yet treat the underlying CTE pathology, our goal is to bend the curve of brain aging, extend brain healthspan and help players feel and function better throughout their lives."

In terms of next steps, the researchers say it will be important to estimate the prevalence of CTE in football players at lower levels of play (high school and college), to help define the scope of this public health concern, but they note the lack of data may make that difficult.
Aside from the statistical challenges, they say we need more research into the mechanisms, clinical manifestations, and prevention of CTE across all levels of play.
The findings are reported in JAMA Network Open.

articles.title: A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuse’s atmosphere, new evidence suggests

paras.en: A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuseâs atmosphere, new evidence suggests

- Something mysterious is disturbing Betelgeuse, and astronomers believe they have identified the culprit: a hidden companion star called Siwarha. New radio observations reveal that the smaller star may be plowing through Betelgeuseâs enormous atmosphere, creating disturbances that subtly stretch and distort the red supergiantâs shape.

Something unusual is happening inside the enormous atmosphere of Betelgeuse, one of the most recognizable stars in the night sky. Astronomers have detected subtle changes in the star's shape that suggest something is moving through its outer layers, disturbing the surrounding gas like an unseen visitor making noise inside a house. (Metaphorically speaking.) New observations point to a likely culprit: Siwarha, a recently discovered companion star that appears to be traveling through Betelgeuse's atmosphere.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Betelgeuse is a massive red supergiant located in the constellation Orion, where it forms the famous hunter's shoulder. Although the star has fascinated astronomers for generations, it attracted worldwide attention in late 2019 and early 2020 when its brightness unexpectedly plunged to its lowest recorded level in more than 100 years. The event, known as the Great Dimming, raised questions about what was happening inside the aging star.

Now, observations from the U.S. National Science Foundation's Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (NSF VLA) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) reveal that Betelgeuse's vast outer atmosphere has largely returned to normal. More intriguingly, the measurements provide new evidence that a nearby companion star is physically disturbing the giant star's atmosphere.

The research was led by Dr. Lynn D. Matthews, Principal Research Scientist and Assistant Director at MIT Haystack Observatory, working with scientists from the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, the University of Manchester, and the European Southern Observatory. The team analyzed observations gathered between 2021 and 2026 at seven radio frequencies ranging from 22 GHz to 485 GHz.

Different radio frequencies allow astronomers to examine different depths within a star's atmosphere. By combining the observations from both telescopes, the researchers reconstructed the structure of Betelgeuse's outer layers, beginning just above its visible surface and extending outward to several times its radius.

"It was the combination of the incredible data from the NSF VLA and ALMA that gave us a convincing result here," said Matthews. "The fact that we can use these facilities to actually resolve the disks of nearby stars is amazing."
Betelgeuse Recovers From Its Mysterious Great Dimming

The latest measurements also help scientists understand how Betelgeuse has changed since its extraordinary fading episode. Several months before the Great Dimming (when Betelgeuse ejected a billion tons of solar material, partially blocking our view), an earlier investigation led by Matthews detected unusually low temperatures in the star's atmosphere at radio wavelengths.

At the time, researchers suggested that turbulent convection deep inside Betelgeuse may have generated a shock wave that traveled outward and disrupted the surrounding gas. That disturbance could have helped trigger the enormous release of material that later formed dust and obscured part of the star's light.

The new observations indicate that the atmosphere has since warmed to temperatures more typical of Betelgeuse. At a distance of approximately 2.7 times the star's radius, the gas now has a measured brightness temperature of about 3,500 Kelvin (comparable to Betelgeuse's own surface temperature).
Astronomers Discover an Unexpectedly Cold Atmospheric Layer

The researchers also confirmed a feature that scientists had suspected existed for years: a region of unusually cool gas between Betelgeuse's visible surface and its higher atmospheric layer, known as the chromosphere.

Using ALMA at its highest observed frequencies, the team was able to probe closer to the star's surface than previous radio measurements had allowed. The results revealed temperatures falling to approximately 2,200 Kelvin, more than 1,000 degrees below the temperature of the visible surface, or photosphere.

This cool region corresponds to the "MOLsphere," a layer containing molecular gas that astronomers had previously identified primarily through infrared observations. The new radio measurements provide a much more direct examination of this elusive part of Betelgeuse's atmosphere and confirm the long-suspected "temperature minimum."
A Hidden Companion Star May Be Distorting Betelgeuse

One of the most intriguing discoveries involves Siwarha, the smaller star believed to orbit extremely close to Betelgeuse. Astronomers first proposed the companion's existence in 2024 as a possible explanation for a puzzling cycle in which Betelgeuse's brightness changes approximately every 2,100 days. Subsequent direct imaging and spectroscopic observations have provided additional support for the companion's existence.
The name Siwarha reflects its relationship with Betelgeuse. The giant star's name comes from the Arabic expression meaning "the hand of al-Jawza," while Siwarha means "her bracelet."

Unlike a planet or star traveling far from its host, Siwarha is believed to follow an orbit that takes it directly through Betelgeuse's extended atmosphere. Its estimated orbital distance is only about twice the red supergiant's radius.
"This companion is orbiting so close to the star that it actually passes through its extended atmosphere," Matthews explained.

As Siwarha moves along its orbit, it may push through the surrounding gas much like a fast boat cutting through water. The resulting wake could disturb the atmosphere, producing changes that astronomers can detect even though the smaller star itself remains invisible in the radio observations.

In fact, the researchers calculated that Siwarha is likely tens to hundreds of times too faint to be detected directly with the radio measurements they collected. Instead, they searched for indirect evidence of its presence by studying the shape of Betelgeuse's atmosphere.
Betelgeuse's Changing Shape Reveals New Clues

The scientists discovered that Betelgeuse does not always appear perfectly round at radio wavelengths. Its atmosphere sometimes develops a slightly stretched, oval appearance, and the timing of these changes appears to match the expected position of Siwarha.
To investigate this connection, the team measured the atmosphere's departure from a circular shape ("ellipticity") across observations taken at different times.

They found that Betelgeuse tends to look more elongated when Siwarha is expected to be at its greatest apparent separation from the giant star. When the companion is predicted to pass in front of or behind Betelgeuse from our perspective, the atmosphere appears rounder.
This relationship provides compelling evidence that the smaller star may be influencing the shape of Betelgeuse's outer layers through gravity and its physical passage through the gas.

The effect resembles noticing ripples spreading across a pond without being able to see what caused them. Although Siwarha remains too faint to identify directly at radio wavelengths, the changing shape of Betelgeuse's atmosphere may reveal its movement around the larger star.
Future Observations Could Reveal More About Betelgeuse

Despite the promising results, astronomers emphasize that additional observations are necessary to confirm the connection between Siwarha's orbit and the atmospheric distortions. Measurements covering more of the companion's orbital cycle, particularly at radio frequencies that have not yet been studied extensively, could help establish how strongly the smaller star affects Betelgeuse.

More advanced instruments may eventually provide an even clearer picture. The Next Generation Very Large Array, an observatory currently under development, is expected to make detailed studies of nearby stars and their atmospheres much easier.

Such observations could reveal not only how companion stars influence their massive neighbors, but also how aging red supergiants lose material as they approach the final stages of their lives. Understanding these interactions may help astronomers better explain the complicated processes that shape the evolution of enormous stars like Betelgeuse.

The findings were published in The Astronomical Journal in a paper titled "New Spatially Resolved Observations of Betelgeuse from the VLA and ALMA: Evidence for Atmospheric Perturbations from a Close Companion."

- L. D. Matthews, A. K. Dupree, A. M. S. Richards, W. R. F. Dent. New Spatially Resolved Observations of Betelgeuse from the VLA and ALMA: Evidence for Atmospheric Perturbations from a Close Companion. The Astronomical Journal, 2026; 172 (3): 184 DOI: 10.3847/1538-3881/ae953d

articles.title: Scientists trick cancer cells into making the drugs that kill them

paras.en: Scientists trick cancer cells into making the drugs that kill them

- Scientists have developed a promising new cancer-fighting strategy that uses carbon monoxide naturally produced by tumor cells to manufacture powerful drugs inside the cancer cells themselves. Early laboratory experiments suggest the technique could selectively attack cancer while sparing healthy cells, potentially paving the way for safer chemotherapy alternatives.

Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative way to turn a chemical produced by cancer cells into a weapon against them. Instead of delivering toxic drugs throughout the body, their experimental approach uses carbon monoxide released by cancer cells to manufacture anticancer compounds directly inside the cells themselves.

The research, led by Katsunori Tanaka at the RIKEN Pioneering Research Institute (PRI) in Japan, was published in Nature Communications. In laboratory experiments, the team demonstrated that a specially designed compound could trigger drug production inside cancer cells without generating the same toxic substances in healthy cells. Although the technique is still at an early stage, it could eventually provide a way to attack tumors while reducing the harmful side effects associated with conventional cancer treatments.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Turning Cancer's Own Toxic Gas Against It

One of the greatest challenges in cancer treatment is destroying malignant cells without damaging healthy tissue. Traditional chemotherapy can cause serious side effects because its toxic effects are not always limited to tumors. Tanaka and other researchers are investigating more selective strategies that could make cancer treatments safer.

Their long-term goal is to replace the direct delivery of toxic drugs with relatively harmless compounds that become active only after entering cancer cells. These compounds would use substances already present inside tumors to generate therapeutic drugs exactly where they are needed.

Carbon monoxide offers an intriguing opportunity for this approach. Although best known as a poisonous gas produced by sources such as gasoline engines, carbon monoxide is also generated naturally by many types of cancer cells. Because tumors can produce unusually high amounts of the gas, it may serve as a useful biological marker for identifying cancer cells, provided it can be detected.

Scientists in RIKEN's Biofunctional Synthetic Chemistry Laboratory investigated whether they could exploit this difference. Their strategy involved delivering a metal catalyst into cells and using the excess carbon monoxide in cancer cells to drive a chemical reaction that produces a toxic compound. In principle, the reaction would occur primarily in cancer cells, where enough carbon monoxide is available, while sparing normal cells.
Protecting the Catalyst Inside Cancer Cells

To make the system work, the researchers turned to a class of compounds known as palladacycles. These metal-containing compounds can react with carbon monoxide to produce an organic molecule called phenanthridinone. Certain derivatives of phenanthridinone are toxic to cells and have already been incorporated into anticancer drugs.

However, there was a major obstacle. When palladacycles are introduced directly into cells, substances such as glutathione rapidly deactivate their central palladium catalyst. Without an active catalyst, the reaction cannot produce the desired drug.

Tanaka's team addressed this problem by building on its previous work using metal catalysts to carry out chemical reactions in living systems. The researchers enclosed a palladacycle within albumin, a protein commonly found in blood. This protective protein carrier allows the complex to travel through the bloodstream while shielding the palladium catalyst from substances that would otherwise deactivate it after entering cells.
Laboratory Tests Reveal Selective Drug Production
The scientists evaluated their system through a series of experiments. They began by testing different palladacycles to identify which one could generate the greatest amount of phenanthridinone.

Next, they exposed cultured human liver, cervical, breast, and lung cancer cells to the albumin and palladacycle complex for 48 hours. They also tested the compound on a noncancerous cell line to determine whether the same chemical reaction would occur in healthy cells.

After 48 hours, the researchers detected phenanthridinone in the cancer cell lines but not in the normal cells. The findings indicated that the albumin carrier successfully protected the catalyst from glutathione and that the chemical reaction occurred selectively in the cancer cells under the conditions tested.

The team then refined the system so that the newly formed compound could separate from the carrier and move freely throughout the cell. Additional modifications allowed the reaction to generate a particularly toxic phenanthridinone derivative already used in anticancer drugs.

When the researchers introduced this modified system into cultured liver cancer cells, they observed the anticancer compound forming inside the cells. The cells subsequently showed signs of damage caused by the toxic drug, providing proof that the approach could generate a cancer-fighting substance directly within its intended target.
Why the Experimental Drug Did Not Form in Blood

An important safety concern involved carbon monoxide already present in the bloodstream. If that gas triggered the chemical reaction before the compound reached cancer cells, the resulting drug could damage blood cells instead of its intended target.

Fortunately, laboratory testing showed that the toxic drug was not produced in blood. The researchers believe this is because carbon monoxide in the bloodstream is largely attached to hemoglobin, the protein responsible for transporting oxygen. In this bound form, the gas appears to be unavailable for the reaction needed to manufacture the drug.

The finding suggests that the system may be able to travel through blood without prematurely generating harmful substances, although further studies will be needed to establish its safety in living organisms.

"This work represents an important advance in therapeutic in vivo synthetic chemistry," says Tanaka. "In our therapeutic strategy, molecules naturally present or generated within the body -- including disease-associated metabolites -- are used as endogenous chemical feedstocks to synthesize therapeutic molecules directly at the site of disease."

The researchers now plan to move beyond cultured cells and test the approach in animal models. If future experiments are successful, the technology could help establish a new class of cancer treatments that exploit the chemistry of tumors to produce drugs directly at the disease site, potentially limiting damage to healthy tissue.
Materials provided by RIKEN. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

- Masayuki Kawai, Tsung-Che Chang, Ambara R. Pradipta, Katsunori Tanaka. Harnessing endogenous carbon monoxide for cancer-selective drug synthesis. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77616-8

articles.title: Gene editing could replace a lifetime of medication, but there's a catch

paras.en: Gene editing could replace a lifetime of medication, but there's a catch
- Michigan Medicine - University of Michigan

- A single gene-editing treatment could someday protect against heart disease, high cholesterol, and other common conditions for decades, potentially replacing lifelong medications. But scientists warn that permanently altering genes introduces risks that could take years to emerge, making long-term safety a critical challenge.

Imagine receiving a single treatment that could keep your cholesterol under control for decades, potentially eliminating the need for daily medication. Advances in gene editing are bringing that possibility closer to reality. But scientists say the same technology that could revolutionize medicine also raises difficult questions about safety, permanent genetic changes, and unintended consequences.

Gene therapy is already being used to treat certain serious illnesses. These treatments can introduce working copies of genes, silence harmful genetic activity, or make changes directly to DNA. Unlike conventional medications that must be taken repeatedly, some genetic treatments are designed to work after just one administration.

More than 6,000 rare genetic disorders have been identified, although only a small proportion currently have targets that can be treated. Gene therapies have already achieved important successes against conditions such as spinal muscular atrophy and sickle cell disease.
Now, researchers are exploring whether similar approaches could help prevent or manage far more widespread health problems, including high cholesterol, heart disease, obesity, and diabetes.
That raises a fundamental question: Just because scientists can permanently change a person's genetic activity, does that mean they should?

In a perspective published in JAMA Internal Medicine, University of Michigan Health Frankel Cardiovascular Center cardiologists Eric D. Smith, M.D., and Venkatesh L. Murthy, M.D., Ph.D., outline how doctors and researchers should weigh the potential benefits of genomic therapies against their risks.

The two gene therapy researchers explain why these treatments are so promising, what makes them different from conventional medicines, and what must happen before they can be safely offered to millions of people.
Why One-Time Gene Therapy Is Different From Daily Medication
One of the most appealing features of gene therapy is the possibility of achieving lasting results without repeated treatments.

Traditional medicines generally work only as long as patients continue taking them. Genomic therapies operate differently because they act on genetic material itself. They may provide a healthy version of a gene, suppress a gene responsible for harmful effects, or modify a specific DNA sequence.
This makes it possible to develop treatments intended to work after a single dose. Such therapies are often called "one-and-done" treatments.
However, receiving a treatment only once does not necessarily mean its effects will last a lifetime.

Smith explains that many gene therapies use modified viruses to carry genetic instructions into cells. The immune system can recognize these delivery vehicles and develop a response against them. As a result, administering the same treatment again may be difficult or impossible, even if its benefits begin to fade.

Another important distinction concerns which cells are changed. Current gene therapies generally target somatic cells, which are the body's cells other than those involved in reproduction. Unlike germline editing, these treatments are not intended to create genetic changes that can be inherited by future generations.
Why Gene Editing Common Diseases Raises New Risks

For people living with rare, devastating genetic conditions, the benefits of gene therapy may clearly outweigh the potential dangers. Some patients have few effective treatment options, making even an experimental intervention worth considering.
The situation becomes considerably more complicated when the same technology is used against common diseases.

Conditions such as high cholesterol, heart disease, obesity, and diabetes already have established treatments. Many of these medications can be adjusted as a patient's condition changes or discontinued if troublesome side effects develop.
A permanent genetic intervention may not offer that flexibility.

Murthy also points to a major concern involving the number of people who might eventually receive these treatments. A serious side effect that occurs only rarely could still harm a substantial number of patients if a therapy is administered to millions.
For that reason, treatments intended for widespread use must meet especially demanding safety standards.
Five Questions Scientists Say Must Be Answered
To help determine when genomic therapy is appropriate, Smith and Murthy propose evaluating five essential factors:
- Disease severity: How serious is the condition being treated, and how much could patients benefit?
- Existing treatments: Are there already effective therapies that can be adjusted or discontinued if necessary?
- Treatment durability: Is the targeted tissue suitable for an intervention intended to produce lasting results after one dose?
- Delivery risks: Are the potential dangers associated with delivering the genetic treatment reasonable given the severity of the disease?
- Long-term monitoring: Can researchers reliably track safety and effectiveness over many years, particularly when large numbers of people receive the treatment?
The final question may be especially challenging.

Clinical trials typically involve relatively small groups of patients who are monitored for limited periods. Although these studies can identify many important safety concerns, they may miss extremely rare complications or problems that take years to develop.
Some adverse effects might only become apparent after a treatment has reached a much larger population.
The Problem of Tracking Risks That Could Emerge Years Later
Smith argues that long-term monitoring cannot be treated as an afterthought. It needs to be an essential part of how gene therapies are introduced into medical practice.
Patient registries, which collect information about people receiving particular treatments, have already shown how valuable extended follow-up can be.
However, therapies that could eventually reach millions of patients will require monitoring systems capable of operating on a much larger scale.
These systems must be independent and standardized so researchers can consistently evaluate whether treatments remain effective and whether unexpected health problems appear over time.
Without reliable long-term data, doctors may struggle to determine the full consequences of genetic interventions that cannot easily be reversed.
Could Some Genetic Changes Be Too Risky to Make Permanent?
Another concern is whether certain diseases or biological processes are suitable for permanent treatment at all.
Murthy emphasizes that developing the ability to alter a genetic target does not automatically make doing so the best medical decision.

Some conditions require careful adjustments to medication doses over time. In other cases, the difference between an effective treatment and a harmful one can be extremely small. Changing a biological process too much or too little could create serious complications.
Conventional medications offer an important advantage in these situations because doctors can modify or stop treatment as needed.
Permanent gene therapies generally lack that option.
Scientists may eventually overcome this limitation by developing genetic treatments with built-in biological "off-switches" or other methods for reversing their effects.
Until those approaches have been shown to work reliably, the ability to undo or adjust a treatment remains an important safety advantage of traditional medicine.
The Million-Dollar Challenge Facing Gene Therapy
Safety is not the only barrier to bringing gene editing into mainstream healthcare. Cost could also determine whether these treatments become widely available.
Some existing gene therapies have list prices above $1 million for a single patient, and several cost substantially more.
Such prices may be considered justifiable for certain rare, life-threatening conditions, particularly when treatment options are extremely limited.
But applying similar pricing to diseases affecting millions of people would place enormous financial pressure on healthcare systems.
Smith and Murthy argue that affordability and access must therefore be part of the discussion from the beginning.

Even a highly effective gene therapy could create new healthcare inequalities if only a small percentage of patients could obtain it. Researchers and policymakers must consider not just whether these treatments work, but also whether they can be delivered without making existing disparities worse.
Could One Gene-Editing Treatment Prevent Heart Disease for Decades?
Despite these challenges, the possibility of using gene editing to prevent common diseases is becoming increasingly realistic.
Researchers are already conducting early studies to investigate whether a single genetic treatment can produce long-lasting reductions in LDL, commonly known as "bad," cholesterol.

LDL cholesterol contributes to the buildup of fatty deposits inside arteries, which can increase the risk of heart attacks and other cardiovascular problems. Lowering LDL over extended periods is an important strategy for reducing cardiovascular risk.
If gene editing can safely produce sustained reductions, it could eventually offer a new approach to protecting cardiovascular health without requiring patients to take medication indefinitely.
However, promising early results will not be enough to justify widespread use.

Before these therapies become routine options for common conditions, researchers will need convincing evidence that their benefits last, their risks remain acceptably low over many years, and their costs are manageable. Reliable safeguards will also be essential.
For Smith and Murthy, the objective is not to hold back genetic medicine. It is to make sure that a technology with the potential to transform healthcare is introduced carefully and responsibly.

As gene therapy moves beyond rare disorders toward conditions affecting millions of people, the central challenge will be ensuring that the promise of lasting protection does not come at the expense of long-term patient safety.

articles.title: Voting in space: NASA astronauts cast ballots from International Space Station
articles.author: Mike Wall

paras.en: The three Americans currently living off Earth just made sure their electoral voices were heard.
Anil Menon told us today (Nov. 3) that he and fellow NASA astronauts Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins voted in the U.S. midterm elections from the International Space Station (ISS).

"Yes, you can even vote from space! All three U.S. crew members had the privilege of voting from space station. We filled out an electronic ballot and sent it securely to the election officials," Menon wrote in an X post this morning.
That post included a 29-second video, in which Menon — wearing, like many of us today, an "I voted" sticker — shows us his "voting booth."
It's actually his room on the ISS, Menon explained. "Inside of it is my computer, where I was able to fill out an electronic form and send it to Harris County so I could vote today," he said.
Most NASA astronauts register to vote in Texas' Harris County; it's home to Johnson Space Center in Houston, the agency's human spaceflight hub.

Americans have been able to vote from space since 1997, when Texas passed a law allowing this to happen. The first person to take advantage of the legislation was NASA astronaut David Wolf, who cast his ballot from Russia's Mir space station that same year. (The ISS didn't welcome its first crew until November 2000.)
"Just like any other American away from home, astronauts may fill out a Federal Post Card Application to request an absentee ballot," NASA officials wrote in an astronaut-voting explainer.
The process is somewhat involved, however.

"After an astronaut fills out an electronic ballot aboard the orbiting laboratory, the document flows through NASA's Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System to a ground antenna at the agency's White Sands Test Facility in Las Cruces, New Mexico," they added. "From New Mexico, NASA transfers the ballot to the Mission Control Center at NASA Johnson and then on to the county clerk responsible for casting the ballot. To preserve the vote's integrity, the ballot is encrypted and accessible only by the astronaut and the clerk."

The trio currently share the orbiting lab with four other people — Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk and cosmonauts Anna Kikina, Pyotr Dubrov and Sergey Teteryatnikov. Kutryk and Teteryatnikov are members of Crew-13, whereas Dubrov and Kikina shared the Soyuz with Menon.

articles.title: Ancient star collisions could explain mysterious Little Red Dots and 'impossible' black holes
articles.author: Robert Lea

paras.en: New research suggests that collisions between stars in the early universe were common, which could help explain the rapid growth of supermassive black holes and the existence of strange Little Red Dots seen by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

The team behind this research performed simulations of the early universe and found stellar systems were densely packed, leading to stars frequently slamming into each other. While rapid collisions would have destroyed the stars involved, slower collisions would have led to repeated mergers, creating single over-massive stars, which could collapse and form larger-than-usual black holes at the end of their lives. These could be the seeds of the first supermassive black holes.

Dense stellar environments do still exist in the modern universe at the hearts of galaxies; however, these aren't conducive to the types of collisions that would birth ultra-massive stars. That is because there are already supermassive black holes at the hearts of modern galaxies, and their immense gravitational influence speeds up orbiting stars, meaning collisions that do occur are high-speed and destructive, thus failing to birth overmassive stars.

"Perhaps the strangest outcome of our simulations is that stars can merge repeatedly within the cluster until they form one gigantic star with a mass equal to that of an entire cluster," team member Claire Williams, of the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), said in a statement. "When a star this huge reaches the end of its life, models suggest that it may have no option but to collapse into itself and form a massive black hole."
My, haven't you grown? How did supermassive black holes get so big so fast?
The existence of supermassive black holes before the universe was even 1 billion years old is something that has puzzled astronomers since the JWST started spotting them in 2022.

This is because black holes should need at least 1 billion years to complete the feeding and merger processes that result in a "supermassive" status of possessing millions or billions of times the mass of the sun.
One suggestion put forward by scientists to explain this is that supermassive black holes don't start out from scratch. Instead, they form from black hole seeds called intermediate-mass black holes.

Normally, when a massive star collapses, it births a stellar-mass black hole possessing a mass between 10 and 100 times the mass of the sun. This is considerably smaller than supermassive black holes that dominate the hearts of all modern galaxies with masses millions to billions of times the mass of our star.

Intermediate-mass black holes are thought to sit between these two families of cosmic titans with masses between 100 and 100,000 times that of the sun. The problem is, no single star should have enough mass to collapse and create an intermediate-mass black hole. But that is valid only for the conditions we see in the "modern" 13.8-billion-year-old universe in our immediate cosmic vicinity. Conditions were very different further out into the universe and further back in time.
Indeed, such seeds emerged from these new simulations in environments of dense star clustering, which could solve this mystery by allowing those growth processes to get a head start.

"Dense star clusters provide a natural birthplace for massive black-hole seeds in our model," Williams said. "The same environment that forms the black hole can also provide stars and gas that influence its subsequent growth."

However, this could be a two-for-one deal. The JWST has also been routinely discovering astronomical bodies called Little Red Dots in the early universe. Little Red Dots are curious because they seem to have completely disappeared by the time the cosmos reached 2 billion years old.
Little Red Dots the cosmic elephant in the room
Little Red Dots are extremely compact objects in the early universe that get their moniker from the fact that they look like red dots.

"Little Red Dots are a hot topic in astronomy. You can compare studies of people trying to understand Little Red Dots to the tale of blind people who are trying to describe an elephant by touching it, and each person describes it differently based on what part they’re touching," team member and UCLA researcher Smadar Naoz said. "Our research connects several of those perspectives together and may help us see more of the elephant."
There have been many suggestions about the true nature of these objects, but one theory suggests that they possess a rapidly growing black hole at their hearts.

The team's simulations suggest that Little Red Dots may be dense star clusters that are constantly being rocked by repeated stellar collisions. This results in a very large star, which eventually collapses to become an intermediate-mass black hole.
But if that is the case, why were there no Little Red Dots around to celebrate the 2 billionth birthday of the universe?

Less than 1 billion years after the Big Bang, the universe was devoid of well-ordered spiral galaxies, but was instead filled with dense and chaotic clusters of star birth. As these regions were rocked with frequent star collisions, the conditions were right for ultra-massive stars to form and collapse into intermediate-mass black holes.

However, as the universe cooled and expanded, these sites became the building blocks of far less chaotic galaxies. Thus, if Little Red Dots are chaotic star clusters needed to form intermediate-mass black holes, progress toward an equilibrium state could explain why they suddenly disappeared from the universe. The cosmos just wasn't extreme enough to maintain Little Red Dots anymore.
The team's research was published on Monday (Oct. 26) in the Astrophysical Journal.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

articles.title: NASA asks industry for ideas about saving Hubble Space Telescope
articles.author: Elizabeth Howell

paras.en: NASA is reviving discussions to rescue the Hubble Space Telescope, which is operating well but is on track to reenter Earth's atmosphere about six years from now.

The agency issued a request for information (RFI) on Oct. 29 for "in-space servicing" capabilities, which could include boosting Hubble's orbit (which is naturally degrading due to atmospheric drag), or even a mission to "enhance its capabilities" in some way.

Hubble, which launched in April 1990 in partnership with the European Space Agency, was serviced five times by astronauts on space shuttle missions, the most recent being in 2009. The observatory's groundbreaking achievements include helping to show that the expansion of the universe is accelerating — a discovery that won the Nobel Prize — as well as a swath of finds about planets, galaxies, stars and other parts of the universe.

Hubble also regularly teams up with other telescopes for science work, and its observations have led to the publication of at least 23,000 scientific papers, NASA figures suggest. And, despite its age, Hubble remains in high demand. "Astronomers request about seven times as much observing time as is available each year," the agency stated in September.

Hubble is also widely appreciated by the public. People have long enjoyed and celebrated its iconic images, such as the Eagle Nebula's "Pillars of Creation," a gorgeous shot that has been revisited several times over the decades. As such, this is not the first time in recent years that discussions have opened about keeping the famed observatory running for a while longer.

In 2022, for example, billionaire tech entrepreneur Jared Isaacman proposed using SpaceX hardware to mount a Hubble-servicing mission. (Isaacman also purchased and commanded two crewed SpaceX missions to Earth orbit, which flew in September 2021 and September 2024.) NASA declined, however, citing possible risks to the healthy observatory.

But things have changed, apparently. Isaacman, who in December 2025 became NASA administrator, said in an Oct. 30 agency statement that Hubble's science return means the agency should "be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible" — especially if doing so would be a cost savings compared with launching another mission.

In an Oct. 30 post on X, Isaacman added that it's "still worth exploring the options" and noted that NASA had previously considered "a far lower-cost solution" to keep the observatory flying. "That was then. Still worth the effort — Hubble deserves it," he added.
The new RFI also allows for alternative scenarios, however, which could include a "safe, controlled reentry into Earth's atmosphere or orbital disposal at the end of Hubble's mission."
Hubble will naturally enter the atmosphere in 2033 or 2034 due to orbital drag, so any attempt to service it would have to be in 2032, the agency stated.

Earlier this year, NASA worked with Katalyst Space Technologies on a $30 million mission that aimed to boost the orbit of the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, which is also falling back to Earth due to orbital drag.

That long-shot rescue mission — which was developed quickly to race against accelerated solar activity, which ballooned Earth's atmosphere and increased drag — launched successfully this summer. But control issues prevented Katalyst's LINK spacecraft from meeting up with Swift. Swift is expected to reenter Earth's atmosphere tomorrow (Nov. 4) after 22 years of operations — far past its two-year design lifetime.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

articles.title: Flexell Space Establishes French Subsidiary to Strengthen European Presence
articles.author: Flexell Space

paras.en: – Paris-based FLEXELL SPACE FRANCE SAS creates a local business hub in Europe
– New entity to support ongoing contract and volume-production discussions with European customers, from technical reviews to supply planning

Paris, France – Flexell Space, a space solar solution company, announced the establishment of its French entity, FLEXELL SPACE FRANCE SAS, in Paris to strengthen support for ongoing contract and volume-production discussions with European customers.

The move comes as the company’s business discussions in Europe advance. Flexell Space is currently in talks with multiple European customers regarding collaboration agreements and volume supply of space solar cells and power solutions. Through its local presence, the company aims to accelerate customer communication and strengthen its ability to support business activities ranging from technical reviews to negotiations on supply terms.
- Advancing Contract and Production Discussions with European Customers

Space solar cells require close coordination on performance, dimensions, reliability, and delivery schedules, depending on each customer’s spacecraft design and operating environment. Beyond initial product introductions, discussions involve technical documentation reviews, sample evaluations, environmental test results, and design adjustments. Progressing toward volume supply also requires alignment on production schedules and quality management processes.

Flexell Space said that as discussions with European customers move toward contracts and volume production, a local presence has become increasingly important for responding promptly to customer needs. The French entity will support these activities and serve as a link between European customers and the company’s R&D and manufacturing teams in Korea.

The company plans to deepen engagement with customers and partners across Europe, including France, Germany, Italy, and Lithuania. By gaining a closer understanding of each customer’s development schedule and technical requirements, it aims to facilitate timely decisions and follow-up actions throughout the collaboration process.
- Connecting Next-Generation Space Solar Technology with Production Readiness

Flexell Space develops next-generation tandem solar cells and related power solutions for space applications. Its tandem architecture combines solar cells with different characteristics to deliver the performance, low weight, and cost competitiveness required for space missions.

The company is expanding beyond solar cell development into modules and arrays tailored to customer missions and satellite platforms. Its preparations for commercialization and volume production address not only product performance, but also reliability in the space environment, manufacturing process repeatability, quality management, and supply stability.

With the establishment of its French entity, Flexell Space plans to incorporate feedback from European technical discussions into product development and supply planning more quickly. It will strengthen coordination between its Korean R&D teams and European customers by communicating required specifications and evaluation criteria, while sharing development progress and validation results.
The company will also continue discussions on supply scope, development schedules, production volumes, and delivery timelines to translate ongoing negotiations into concrete business outcomes.
- Building Long-Term Partnerships Across Europe

Flexell Space plans to operate its French entity as a hub for developing long-term relationships with European customers. Alongside supporting existing customer projects, it will explore new product applications and joint development opportunities with local space companies and research institutions.

As satellite missions and platforms become more diverse, space power solutions increasingly require development and supply arrangements tailored to specific operating conditions. Flexell Space’s strategy is to maintain close contact with customers and connect their requirements with R&D and manufacturing preparations to expand its European business.

“We are currently discussing contracts and volume supply with multiple European customers. As these discussions progress, being closer to our customers has become increasingly important in turning them into tangible results,” said Keo-san Lee, CFO of Flexell Space. “Our French entity will help accelerate technical discussions and business execution, while enabling us to respond more closely to our customers’ development and production schedules.”

“In the space industry, technical capability must be accompanied by confidence in a supplier’s ability to deliver products reliably,” Lee added. “By connecting our R&D and manufacturing capabilities in Korea with local customer support in Europe, we aim to build stronger, longer-term partnerships.”

articles.title: Flexell Space and Satoro Agree to Collaborate on In-Orbit Demonstration of Next-Generation Space Solar Cells
articles.author: Flexell Space

paras.en: – Two demonstration missions planned aboard SpaceX Falcon 9, one each in 2027 and 2028
– Satoro to provide “Satellite-as-a-service” solution; Flexell Space to supply solar cells and test modules

Uiwang-si, Korea – Flexell Space, a space energy company led by CEO Taehun Ahn, announced that it has signed an agreement with Singapore-based CubeSat specialist Satoro, led by CEO Mark Lu, for the in-orbit demonstration and validation (IOD/IOV) of next-generation space solar cells.

The agreement aims to verify the performance and reliability of Flexell Space’s solar cells in the actual space environment. The companies plan to conduct two demonstration missions, one in 2027 and another in 2028. Each demonstration satellite is scheduled to launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.

Flexell Space previously conducted two space demonstration missions through launches aboard Korea’s KSLV-II, in November 2025 and October 2026. Building on this experience, the agreement with Satoro will expand opportunities for in-orbit validation of its next-generation space solar cells and support the continued accumulation of operational data needed for commercialization.

Under the agreement, Satoro will manufacture the satellites for the demonstration missions, while Flexell Space will supply the solar cells and test modules to be integrated into them. The companies will coordinate technical requirements for the CubeSat platforms and demonstration payloads, working together to evaluate the solar cells’ operating characteristics and performance in orbit.

Through these missions, Flexell Space plans to compare and validate ground-test results against in-orbit operational data and assess the solar cells’ power output characteristics and performance changes over time. Data collected from both missions will support further design improvements and reliability validation, strengthening the technical foundation for evaluations by global customers and future commercial supply.

The collaboration brings together Satoro’s expertise in CubeSat manufacturing and demonstration missions with Flexell Space’s capabilities in next-generation solar cell development. Flexell Space is developing solar cell technologies based on CIGS (copper indium gallium selenide) and perovskites, with a focus on commercializing low-cost, large-area, ultralight power solutions for satellites and a wide range of space infrastructure.

“Commercializing space solar cells requires both ground-based performance validation and data collected in orbit,” said Taehun Ahn, CEO of Flexell Space. “With two demonstration opportunities secured for 2027 and 2028, we will systematically verify the performance and reliability of our next-generation solar cells and build the technical evidence required by global customers.”
He added, “Our collaboration with Satoro establishes a clear path from development to in-orbit demonstration and will accelerate our preparations for future commercial supply.”

“We are pleased to work with Flexell Space on the demonstration of its next-generation space solar cells,” said Mark Lu, CEO of Satoro. “Drawing on Satoro’s CubeSat platforms and mission integration capabilities, we will work closely with Flexell Space to help secure the in-orbit data needed to validate its technology.”

He added, “We look forward to these two demonstration missions advancing the commercial potential of new space power technologies and laying the groundwork for continued technical collaboration between our companies.”

Flexell Space is a space energy company that originated as an internal venture at Hanwha Systems and develops next-generation space solar cells and power solutions. The company focuses on low-cost, large-area, ultralight products based on CIGS and perovskite solar cell technologies, with an emphasis on the durability, radiation tolerance, and long-term operational reliability required for space applications. Through collaboration with global satellite manufacturers and space agencies, Flexell Space is advancing the commercialization of solar cell technologies for satellites and space infrastructure.

articles.title: Before the Dawn in America’s Heartland

paras.en: The predawn hours brought clear skies over much of the eastern United States on October 18, 2026. An astronaut aboard the International Space Station seized the opportunity to capture this wide-angle photo at 4:54 a.m. Central Daylight Time (09:54 Universal Time), with illuminated cities large and small arrayed across the darkened landscape.

The U.S. Midwest’s largest metropolitan areas, such as Chicago, Illinois, and Detroit, Michigan, stand out as some of the brightest features. Mid-sized cities—including Indianapolis, Indiana; Cincinnati, Ohio; and Louisville, Kentucky—and their interconnections along state and interstate highways also shine brightly.

Above the web of nighttime lights and Earth’s lower atmosphere, a diffuse layer of green and orange is visible along the horizon to the left. This band of light is airglow, produced when sunlight strikes atoms and molecules in the upper atmosphere and causes them to eject photons. To the right, light from the Sun arcs across the horizon; sunrise was about an hour away on the East Coast and about two hours away in Chicago.

Astronaut photos and other remote sensing observations of nighttime lights are scientifically valuable for tracking changes in the built environment. For example, Chicago's lightscape appears a homogeneous pale yellow in the wide view above. But in detailed photos, like the one below, a range of colors stemming from different types of lighting is discernible. Using NASA’s extensive Gateway to Astronaut Photography of Earth archive, researchers have developed a method for distinguishing lighting types within the pixels of nighttime photos. Systematically quantifying urban lights’ brightness, color, and extent can provide insight into how cities grow and evolve.

paras.en: Satellite sensors also observe changes to lighting. In particular, NASA’s Black Marble nighttime lights product suite uses satellite observations to produce science-quality records of nighttime lights across the globe at daily, monthly, and yearly time scales. In the eastern U.S., scientists have used these data to track everything from power outages and restoration following major storms to lighting changes associated with new infrastructure to transitions to LED lighting from older forms.

They are provided by the ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit at NASA Johnson Space Center. The images were taken by members of the Expedition 75 and Expedition 70 crews, respectively. The images have been cropped and enhanced to improve contrast, and lens artifacts have been removed. The International Space Station Program supports the laboratory as part of the ISS National Lab to help astronauts take pictures of Earth that will be of the greatest value to scientists and the public, and to make those images freely available on the internet.
