articles.title: Married off at 14: In Yemen’s war, women and girls suffer ‘devastating consequences’

paras.en: Married off at 14: In Yemen’s war, women and girls suffer ‘devastating consequences’

Safa is 14. Her mother died earlier this year. She has no brothers or sisters. And a few weeks ago, as the crisis took hold, her father married her to an elderly man, afraid that if he were killed in the hostilities, no one would be left to protect her.

“Safa’s words show how war can strip away protection at every turn,” Francesco Galtieri, the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) Representative in Yemen, told journalists in Geneva on Tuesday, speaking via video link from Aden.
Hers is “a stark reminder of the impossible choices some families are facing and the devastating consequences, particularly for girls,” he said.

Fighting in parts of Yemen has intensified to levels not seen since 2020, and displacement from the west coast and Taiz has tripled: nearly 300,000 people have been driven from their homes, more than half of them women and children.
More than a third of the displaced families are led by a woman.

In the displacement sites where they land, women and girls face heightened risks of sexual violence, harassment, exploitation, and forced and child marriage; threats that – layered on top of loss and uncertainty – are wearing down their mental and psychosocial health.
In Taiz city, the midwives are among the first to see to toll the war is taking.

Severely malnourished pregnant women, they report, are surviving on one or, at most, two meals a day – “a cup of tea or some bread and plain rice”. Miscarriages are rising, and more women are giving birth at home, unsafely.

Of the more than 13,000 pregnant women in the Taiz area, some 6,400 have been displaced. Among those women, UNFPA expects roughly 1,500 obstetric emergencies, caused by the toll of walking for safety while pregnant, carrying children and whatever could be saved.
“No woman should have to risk her life simply because she’s giving birth to a new life in a war zone,” Mr. Galtieri said.
At the Swedish Motherhood and Childhood Hospital, the main maternal care facility in the city, the rate of survival is shrinking. Deliveries have halved, from ten a day to about five.

Incubators for premature babies are down from 40 to ten for want of fuel. Nighttime admissions have fallen to almost zero, because insecurity and shelling keep women from travelling, while health workers struggle to reach the wards at all.
Unless access restrictions are lifted in the coming days, Mr. Galtieri warned, “the hospital itself could close”.
Across Taiz, only five of 27 designated emergency maternal and newborn hospitals are even partially functioning.
Before this escalation, an estimated three women died in childbirth every day in Yemen, which has the highest maternal mortality rate in the Arab region.

UNFPA and its partners are responding wherever access allows. Some 129 community midwives seek out pregnant women in the areas they cover while five mobile teams deliver reproductive health and protection services.

But too often, Mr. Galtieri said, the needs of women and girls are the first to be overlooked and the last to be heard. Societies praise women’s resilience without standing by their side in any tangible way.
“Their voices must not disappear behind the statistics of war.”

articles.title: World News in Brief: Children killed in Myanmar strike, new violence flares in Mozambique, an Internet affordability milestone

paras.en: World News in Brief: Children killed in Myanmar strike, new violence flares in Mozambique, an Internet affordability milestone
The educational centre in Loikaw Township, Kayah state was being used by displaced families when it came under attack on Saturday, amid an ongoing civil war sparked by a coup in 2021.
Further airstrikes were reported in Rakhine state over the weekend, including one that struck a temporary healthcare facility, reportedly killing a newborn baby and healthcare workers.
“These reports are yet another stark reminder that children are bearing the brunt for the devastating conflict in Myanmar,” UNICEF said.
It added that youngsters “are being killed and injured in the very places where they should be safe and protected.”
The agency issued an appeal to all parties to the conflict to uphold their obligations under international humanitarian law and take all necessary measures to protect children.
Mozambique: More than 7,000 flee fresh violence in Cabo Delgado

More than 7,000 people have fled their homes in northern Mozambique’s Cabo Delgado province since late September, escaping fresh violence and fear of attacks by non-state armed groups, according to new data from the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
Nearly 80 per cent of the latest arrivals are women and children. Many are seeking safety in communities that already host people displaced by years of conflict.
“These communities need help with food, shelter and healthcare,” said Dana Graber Ladek, IOM Chief of Mission in Mozambique.
“Without timely support, life could get much harder for displaced families and the people hosting them.”
Between 21 September and 13 October, 5,794 people were displaced, followed by another 1,235 between 14 and 27 October. Some have had to flee more than once.

In the most recent two weeks, those displaced included 87 pregnant women, 58 older people, 18 people with disabilities and four unaccompanied or separated children. Many men stayed behind to keep earning a living, despite the danger.
Cabo Delgado already hosts more than 205,000 displaced people across 84 sites. More than half of them are children.
Food is the most urgent need, reported by 88 per cent of those assessed, followed by shelter (71 per cent) and healthcare (44 per cent).

The UN migration agency is providing emergency shelter, household items, water, sanitation and hygiene, protection and psychosocial support. But it warned that continued displacement and falling funding are stretching the response just as needs grow.
Affordability of mobile internet reaches new milestone

Mobile internet has become affordable in the world’s landlocked developing countries and small island developing States for the first time, according to new figures released on Tuesday by the UN’s International Telecommunication Union (ITU).
The median price of a basic mobile data plan in both groups has fallen below the internationally agreed target of 2 per cent of average income.
“In the age of AI, being offline means being shut out of countless opportunities, from education to employment,” said ITU Secretary-General Doreen Bogdan-Martin.
Some 6.3 billion people – 76 per cent of the world’s population – are online this year, up from 6.1 billion in 2025, though 2 billion remain unconnected.
Prices remain stubbornly high in the least developed countries, at 6.1 per cent of income, and three in 10 economies meet neither the mobile nor the fixed broadband target.

Connection quality varies too. 5G networks reach 86 per cent of people in high-income countries but just 4 per cent in low-income ones. There, the average mobile user gets through 3.4 GB of data a month – around six times less than in richer nations.
“Now more than ever, we need to expand connectivity and make it meaningful for everyone, everywhere,” Ms. Bogdan-Martin said.

articles.title: ‘This is not about politics. This is about people’: UN warns of impact of deadly drone strikes in Sudan

paras.en: ‘This is not about politics. This is about people’: UN warns of impact of deadly drone strikes in Sudan

Intensifying drone attacks on civilian infrastructure across Sudan are disrupting electricity, water and fuel supplies, putting lives at risk and hampering the delivery of humanitarian aid, the UN’s top official in the country has warned.
Hundreds of aid trucks are stranded due to fuel shortages, while hospitals are struggling to maintain lifesaving services, including dialysis.

Speaking to UN News, UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator Denise Brown urged the international community to intervene to end the fighting and provide urgently needed funding, saying: “This is not about politics. This is about people.”
UN News: Let me begin by asking about the escalating drone attacks and their devastating impact on civilians. What are you seeing on the ground?

Denise Brown: There's been an intense pattern of drone strikes over the past couple of weeks. What we're seeing is what appear to be targeted attacks on civilian infrastructure, which, of course, is protected under international humanitarian law.
Sources of energy and fuel appear to be systematically targeted and destroyed. So already there's an apparent violation here.

Essential services are also being massively disrupted. Colleagues from the World Health Organization (WHO) were at a hospital just outside Khartoum, and the electricity went out because of these drone strikes. The hospital has no generator, no solar panels. So, the 25 people who need dialysis had their treatment stopped, point blank.
There was nothing they could do without electricity. This affects women giving birth, children and everyone else. The same goes for water. There are also widespread fuel shortages.
In Khartoum, there are queues kilometres long as people wait for fuel. But what we're seeing is tuk-tuk drivers – those who take people to work and to the market.

These are people who earn a daily wage and are having to wait several days in a row to get fuel, which means they're not earning an income. That's the direct impact of the widespread intensification of drone strikes and their immediate consequences for the civilian population.
We've also seen markets and displacement sites being hit. So, the attacks are widespread and, I have to say, increasingly worrying for us and scarring for the population.
UN News: Amid this escalation, can you tell us more about the UN's response on the ground and its main priorities right now?

Denise Brown: The UN humanitarian community works alongside international and national non-governmental organizations and local communities. It's the communities who are always the first to respond and who are consistently on the front line. But we have one priority, which is to save lives.
Because of the severe rainfall deficits over the past couple of months, we now have a new dimension to what is already a pre-existing catastrophe, quite frankly.

Farmers have been faced with a lack of rainfall, so we know that in some parts of Darfur and Kordofan, people are on the move looking for food. But that's just an additional layer; it's not the only factor we're dealing with.

We have millions of people displaced who continue to be displaced because of the war. Basic social services have been disrupted, and the health system, despite best efforts, has been decimated. Severe acute malnutrition, as we know from the UN Children Fund (UNICEF)’s studies, is very high, exceeding the emergency threshold in many parts of the country, particularly those directly affected by the war.
Our priority is to work with partners to provide services and supplies to people who, very frankly speaking, would die without that assistance.
UN News: What are your greatest concerns at this point?

Denise Brown: The UN has a very big supply chain for food, nutritious products, shelter and non-food items. That's really one of the added values of the UN humanitarian response. But we have hundreds of trucks stuck because of a lack of fuel.

Sometimes we face bureaucratic impediments, which we work with the authorities to overcome, and there's been huge progress regarding our visas and permits. Hopefully that continues, and I expect it will. But honestly, if we don't have fuel, we can't move.
We can't provide food to people who need it, or support children suffering from severe acute malnutrition. A person has had to leave her house, and we don't have a tent to provide for her.
So, I have multiple worries, and this is starting to become a really big one.
UN News: Beyond fuel shortages, what other significant constraints are UN agencies and their partners facing on the ground? And how are funding cuts affecting the response?
Denise Brown: We are in an active war zone, so there are no easy days here. Everything is difficult. We troubleshoot and solve problems constantly.

Very, very unfortunately, the World Food Programme (WFP), which moves thousands of trucks across this country carrying food for people who need it when local markets don't have food available, has had seven hits on its convoys just this year, and 20 over the past two years.
That results in loss of life and loss of food that was intended for the people who needed it most.

Of course, it's a very difficult way for us to operate. So, we must navigate these risks, and we do that daily, trying to reach people in very difficult places like Dilling in South Kordofan, or parts of Blue Nile, Darfur and West Kordofan.
It's a constant negotiation to make sure we can get people and supplies in safely and support the local communities on the frontlines.
UN News: Turning to the protection of civilians and the prevention of further violations, what role does the UN play in strengthening protection on the ground?

Denise Brown: Our role within the country is different from our role outside the country. Within the country, our role is to make sure we are present where people need us. Protection by presence, so that we're there, we understand what's going on, and we can have conversations with communities. Is it the drone strikes? Is it women and children alone?
This war and the reports of conflict-related sexual violence surrounding the atrocities in El-Fasher in October 2025 are sky-high.

We're talking about thousands and thousands of incidents of conflict-related sexual violence. We discuss our concerns very clearly with the authorities here and with the other actors. It is the responsibility of the UN humanitarian community to engage with all actors, and we do that and share those concerns.

But I think now, with the escalation of the drone strikes, and I don't know where those drone strikes are originating from, we need help passing the message to whoever needs to hear it, that this must stop.

There is no defence for repeatedly hitting power stations and fuel stations. People who need lifesaving dialysis can't get it. Women are giving birth with no lights in the hospital. Operations can't take place.

First and foremost, it is the responsibility of those sending the drone strikes. And then it is up to UN Member States to understand what's going on here and really, really work to temper the current situation.
UN News: Finally, what is your message to the international community and regional actors?
Denise Brown: I could give you a whole list of how difficult it is here, but I can also tell you that we are able to deliver.

We are very respectful of the local communities, local organizations, international and national NGOs and UN agencies who work under very difficult circumstances. But we've demonstrated that we can do our job.
We need to be funded to do more. WFP is cutting not just the number of people it serves in Sudan, but also its rations.

I was in a camp in Abu Shandi in Blue Nile a couple of weeks ago, and people said to me, “We need food.” And I had to tell them, “Please be patient.” How can I tell people to be patient and wait for food? How does that happen? They have no money. They've left everything behind. They need us, and we need the donors.
This is not about politics. This is about people. It's about putting the people of Sudan front and centre of what is going on and making sure that at least we're taking care of their basic needs.

articles.title: Billam-Smith grudge with Clarke revealed | 'It affected him for years'

paras.en: Chris Billam-Smith amateur grudge with Cheavon Clarke revealed | 'Only nine minutes but it affected his life for years'

Chris Billam-Smith fights Cheavon Clarke at the Copper Box Arena on Saturday live on Sky Sports; Billam-Smith's rivalry with Clarke dates back more than 10 years; Clarke beat him in an amateur bout that had profound consequences for both boxers; Now they look to settle the score
Old wounds can still ache. Chris Billam-Smith has achieved more than Cheavon Clarke as a professional fighter. But Clarke still has something Billam-Smith never got.
They fight each other on Saturday in the headline bout at the Copper Box Arena in London, live on Sky Sports.
10 years ago, when they were amateur boxers, Clarke beat Billam-Smith in the final of the national championships.
The result spun their lives in different directions. It led Clarke onto the GB squad, where he excelled and became an Olympian.
Billam-Smith never did win the elites. He eventually turned professional, labouring on small hall shows at first though he rose to win British, Commonwealth, European and ultimately a world title.
But losing to Clarke in that 2016 amateur final, one of Billam-Smith's two amateur losses to him, hurt.

At the time Billam-Smith craved the national title. He'd reached the final three years before and at that point in 2016 he was favoured to finally win it. It would have been his gateway to the Olympic programme.
Instead Clarke, who'd drifted away from boxing before making an unheralded return, supplanted him as the country's amateur No 1.
At the end of that intense three-round encounter, Clarke had his hand raised and danced in the ring as he took his victory.
"I was dancing like a madman," Clarke recalled. "When I think about, if I didn't win that, would I have got the opportunity to go on the national team?
"Chev Clarke was not supposed to be in the final. On the way to the final I beat all the favourites that year."
"I wouldn't dance as my celebration," Billam-Smith sighed, "but he won his fight, he can celebrate how he wants."
What Billam-Smith wants is revenge. It's not easy beating a fighter who has already beaten you, but Billam-Smith did that with Richard Riakporhe. He is determined to settle the score with Clarke too.

"Amateur and pro is a different sport and had I not changed enough as a pro and I was still that out-and-out boxer then this fight, and my outlook on it, would be different," Billam-Smith told Sky Sports.
"But I'm a completely fighter to how I was then, on the backfoot boxing long as an amateur. Now I'm on the front foot punching short. It's literally the opposite."
But it's not just the technical challenge of solving the problems this opponent poses, it's the emotional satisfaction he wants.
"There's probably someone better at psychology than me [who can say] as to why I enjoy avenging a defeat," Billam-Smith said.
"I've always had this inner competitive spirit where I want to win and that's what's got to me to the stage I'm at. Because I want to win.

"I've got that in me. To then lose and then avenge it, that's a great feeling. Especially when you've lost a fight, you're the underdog going into the next fight, most of the time. This fight will be different because of the scenario."
Clarke though showed how dangerous he can be in his last fight, when he picked himself up from the deck twice to take out Jack Massey, a former European champion and world title challenger.

Billam-Smith noted: "With Chev he keeps the speed [when hurt] and that's why he was able to land that right hand that was the beginning of the end for Jack and that makes him a really, really dangerous fight. Really dangerous.
"At the same time I believe in my own abilities but I'm very aware of the other possibilities and what could happen if I'm not on my game."
But he added: "I love that feeling, that fear of a big puncher can make you perform well and with Chev it's definitely that."
Clarke has something to prove himself in their upcoming fight on Saturday. He's seen Billam-Smith overhaul and eclipse him as a professional. He's the underdog in this fight.
It reminds him of that amateur championship. "I think it's the same thing, the fact that people wrote me off all the way through," he said.
"My story is still being written. I come out and I set myself a goal. I'm willing to do whatever it takes with integrity to achieve it.
"Come November 7, he's got his bitterness and I've got my attitude. So you guys are in for a hell of fight."
Current European champion Viddal Riley boxed Billam-Smith as an amateur and Clarke as a pro. He understands Billam-Smith's grudge. It's something that lingers.

"It definitely does because it has such a knock-on effect to even what your pro career journey starts off as. Chev starts his pro journey as an Olympian, getting promoted as such, A side," Riley told Sky Sports.

"Chris would have had to get out the mud. He had to get out the mud. It affected his life for years despite that fight being only nine minutes. So it's interesting. I think Chris will have that in his heart going into this weekend.
"He's had that chip on his shoulder and he's done extremely well with that chip on his shoulder because he's won every belt you can win.
"Chev will also know that he needs to win to be a force to be reckoned with in the division. Otherwise he's going to be on the outskirts of the juicy fights."

articles.title: Wolff: 'Good person' Antonelli should be a role model for entitled F1 drivers

paras.en: Toto Wolff says 'good person' Kimi Antonelli should be a role model for 'entitled' Formula 1 drivers ahead of Sao Paulo Grand Prix

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff lauded Kimi Antonelli and stated the new world champion "represents the modern Formula 1 driver"; watch Friday's practice sessions at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix from 3.30pm and 7pm, live on Sky Sports F1
Mercedes boss Toto Wolff says newly crowned world champion Kimi Antonelli should be a role model for both upcoming drivers and some of his “entitled” Formula 1 rivals.
The 20-year-old Italian become the sport's youngest ever world champion as he wrapped up the title with four rounds to spare at Sunday's Mexico City Grand Prix.
Antonelli has not only produced a historic campaign in just his second season in F1, but has also charmed his Mercedes colleagues, rivals, and fans with his charm and youthful exuberance.
- How Mercedes can win Constructors' Championship this Sunday
- Sao Paulo GP Schedule on Sky | F1 2026 Calendar | F1 2026 Standings
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺
At the end of his briefing with the written media in Mexico following the race, Wolff gave an unpromoted impassioned speech praising Antonelli.
"This notion of win at all costs, selfish, opportunistic, ruthless for your own benefit. That model of racing driver has died," Wolff said.
"We have a new champion that represents values - humility, integrity, loyalty, respect. Being himself. He should be a role model for many other young drivers in junior formulas.
"He should be a role model for the few entitled ones in Formula 1 - the endless moaners on the radio, the ones that complain, the ones that crash.
"Look at this kid of 20 years [old] and then think what you can do in order to improve. That's the message to these kids.
"That is how the FIA, that Mohammed [Ben Sulayem], that Stefano [Domenicali], that's how I would want to see racing drivers in the future.
"That is modern Formula 1. Kimi represents the modern Formula 1 driver because of those values, not only because of his talent.
"The talent is there with everyone. But you have got to be a good person too. He has demonstrated that you can beat everyone out there by being a good person."
Antonelli only needed to finish in the top nine in Mexico to seal the title, but produced a strong drive to finish on the podium behind race winner Max Verstappen, and Lewis Hamilton.
Hamilton shares the record for the most F1 titles on seven, while Verstappen has four, and after the race Antonelli appeared to already be thinking about joining them as multiple world champions.
Antonelli told Sky Sports F1: "This is just the beginning. This win is just going to mark a new beginning, a new point to build on to keep improving and to keep trying to win championships.
"Obviously it's been incredible to share the podium with Max and Lewis and hopefully there will be many more battles with them in the future."

Antonelli failed to meet expectations at times during his rookie campaign last season, with a poor run of results during the European summer leading many to question Mercedes' decision to fast-track him into one of the sport's most desirable seats after Hamilton's switch to Ferrari.
The Italian admitted he has enjoyed silencing his critics with his remarkable jump forward this season.

"It's always good to shut off some of the noise. Of course, I think in many ways it does help to add fuel to the fire, the fact that some people said that I wasn't belonging to Formula 1 or I wasn't ready for it, which, at some point last year, probably looked like that I wasn't ready for it," said Antonelli.

"But I think last year, being able to experience those moments made me much more ready as well ahead of this year. I think experiencing really low and difficult situations, high-pressure moments, really helped me to face certain situations this year, and definitely they made me mature a lot as a driver and as a person.
"And still this year, I've had moments where I could have done better, a lot better. So, yeah, it's just a constant learning process.
"But I think last year, being able to race straight into Mercedes, obviously straight under the spotlight, made me grow much, much faster than if I would have gone to a smaller team, for example."

articles.title: Stores looted in German riots as Gen Z activists protest living costs, military service
articles.author: Freddie Clayton

paras.en: Rioters looted stores and set fires to barricades in Frankfurt on Saturday as protests across Germany demanded lower living costs and better education.

Tens of thousands of people across more than 30 cities took to the streets, including in the capital Berlin and financial hub Frankfurt, in protests organized by the campaign group Gen Z Regelt (Gen Z Takes Charge).
The activists demand spending on schools, climate protection and housing, and are against plans to return to mandatory military service.
But the largely peaceful protests, which coincided with Halloween and came weeks after some of the worst rioting in decades erupted in neighboring France, turned violent in some areas.

“In the city center, windows have been smashed at several shops,” Frankfurt police said on X. “Molotov cocktails are also being thrown at the emergency services. We urge all bystanders to avoid the city center or to leave the area.”
In Hamburg, some barricades were set on fire. Some businesses had boarded up their windows and doors in preparation for the protests.

“We are here today to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion,” Gen Z Regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said in Berlin on Saturday. “What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favor of a fairer distribution of the burden.”
Official numbers Saturday afternoon suggested turnout was below the 182,000 participants that organizers initially expected.
The protests took place alongside many others in Europe.

France, Italy, Serbia and Spain have seen protests against the cost of living, among other causes. In France, student protests about the state of education last month evolved into wider demonstrations about the cost of living and social security.
As the demonstrations began Saturday afternoon in Paris, protesters were pictured holding a banner that read: “We do not need tear gas for our future to be blurry.”
Videos vetted by NBC News show large crowds and fires burning in Marseille.
Roman Poseck, interior minister for the German state of Hesse, which includes Frankfurt, warned Germans against using protests in France as an example ahead of Saturday’s protests.
“We all have those images from France in our minds — looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles and attacks on police officers,” he said. “France must not be held up as a model in this regard.”
France’s Interior Ministry said turnout stood at 320,000 on Saturday.

In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government also said it would deploy 500 army troops alongside the police in Milan until the end of the year after masked groups looted stores in the fashion capital and elsewhere and threw projectiles at police earlier this month.
Tens of thousands of people again took to the streets of Rome and other cities and towns across the country Friday.
The demonstrations were largely peaceful, but an NBC News crew saw police use a water cannon on protesters and groups of police charging to disperse protesters.
In Serbia, student-led activism also helped unseat the country’s longtime leader at the ballot box.
Meanwhile, police in Portugal early Sunday forcibly cleared a tent camp set up in Lisbon by activists protesting high housing costs.
Hundreds of protesters shielding the tent camp were dispersed by police using shields and some baton charges, the Reuters news agency reported.

While the protests across the continent have drawn comparisons for their timing, Andrew Barclay, a politics lecturer at the University of Sheffield in England, said it was important to focus on their differences.
The French protests have involved “hundreds of thousands taking to the streets over many weeks, and at least initially centered on specific grievances about education funding,” he told NBC News.

While protests elsewhere may have taken inspiration from the French, he said, “their scale so far hasn’t been as large, and whilst the state of education continues to be a common theme, the issues being protested has ballooned to include a much larger number of complaints.”
Similarly, Barclay said, the protests in Germany and France were unlikely to lead to a direct change in governance as they did in Serbia.

“Often protests, even quite large ones, don’t capture that level of support elsewhere in the country,” he said. “I would be very cautious about comparing what we have seen in Serbia, where students and others have organized to oppose state corruption, to the sorts of protests that we are seeing elsewhere.”

articles.title: Minor detained after U.S. warned Russia of possible Moscow terrorist attack, FSB says
articles.author: NBC News

paras.en: Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) said it had received information from the U.S. through established partner channels about preparations for a terrorist attack in Moscow.

The FSB said Sunday that it had “verified” the information received from U.S. law enforcement and that “as a result of these operations, a Russian minor was detained,” Russia’s Tass state news agency reported.

It said that a person “had posted photos on the short-video platform TikTok showing himself wearing tactical gear—including a balaclava, a cap, protective eyewear, and headphones—while holding an object resembling an automatic weapon.”

A search of his devices revealed a “subscription to a neo-Nazi channel on the messaging app Telegram, and a significant number of search queries concerning past terrorist attacks, mass shootings, and other acts of violence,” Tass reported, citing the FSB.

The U.S. Embassy in Moscow said that it was “aware of a credible threat of a mass casualty event” Saturday at Moscow’s Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve and that the U.S. government was coordinating with Russian authorities.

The Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve, a palace museum and park complex south of Moscow, was temporarily closed Saturday and access to the park was restricted, the RIA news agency reported, citing Russian law enforcement agencies.

The Russian tabloid Baza reported that the venue was evacuated toward the end of an organ concert, which was cut short with about 10 minutes left in the program. A separate concert dedicated to the folk traditions of the North Caucasus region was subsequently canceled, the newspaper reported.

In March 2024, the U.S. Embassy warned that extremists had imminent plans for an attack in Moscow. Days later, gunmen attacked the Crocus City Hall concert venue outside Moscow, killing more than 140 people.

articles.title: Israel’s president says parties need to engage with ‘open heart’ to avoid fresh election
articles.author: Freddie Clayton

paras.en: Israeli President Isaac Herzog has urged the country’s political parties to enter negotiations on forming a new government with an “open heart,” as he prepares to consult with factions on a path forward after an uncertain election result.
Last week’s elections saw Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc denied a majority, with the parties in his ruling coalition claiming 53 seats in Israel’s 120-member Knesset.
Parties in the bloc aligned with Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, won 48 seats, leaving neither man with an obvious path to forming a government.

The balance of power is held by parties representing Israel’s minority Arab community, which nearly doubled its representation in Israel’s parliament with 19 seats. But both Netanyahu and Eisenkot had ruled out working with them prior to the vote.

Netanyahu has since continued to attack the Arab parties, accusing them of holding stances on Gaza and the West Bank he considers unacceptable. Eisenkot, however, has indicated he is open to working with anyone who agrees to four conditions on Israeli sovereignty and opposition to Hamas, potentially opening a path to a deal that could propel him to power and avoid fresh elections.

While Netanyahu is the leader of the single largest party, it is up to Herzog — largely a ceremonial figure — to decide who has the first shot at forming a government. He will hold initial consultations with party officials Wednesday, beginning a delicate process that could last weeks.

“I hope the representatives will come with an open mind, and today I add: with an open heart,” Herzog said in a statement Sunday. “Come to listen and to be heard, to share ideas, and to find creative solutions to prevent another round of elections.”

Netanyahu, who is set to remain in his post as a caretaker until a new government can be formed, has claimed Arab parties used foreign backing to “steal” the elections, without providing evidence. Israeli intelligence agency Shin Bet has said it is investigating possible foreign interference in the election but that the probe was not intended to “cast aspersions” on any specific group.
Arab party leaders have strongly denied any wrongdoing, while Herzog pushed party leaders to accept the election result.

“During an election campaign, candidates naturally and predictably climb to lofty positions,” Herzog said in his statement. “But the elections are over. The election results are a fact. They are a reality. And now is the time to call on all our leaders to stop climbing and face this reality.”

The four conditions Eisenkot set out for prospective partners include recognizing Israel as a Jewish state, committing to the values of its independence, accepting mandatory military service for all Israeli citizens and recognizing Hamas as a terrorist organization.

“Every Knesset member who is willing to sign on to these principles is a potential partner on the path to establishing a new and better government for Israel,” he said in a statement Saturday. “The door to the government we will form will be open to every public representative who accepts these principles and is ready to rise to the occasion.”
Netanyahu, meanwhile, said Sunday that it was “forbidden” to form a government with Mansour Abbas, head of Arab-led party Ra’am.

He said on X that Abbas wants to establish a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital and evacuate Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories, citing an old Ra’am policy platform.
During the campaign, Netanyahu’s Likud party repeatedly alleged that Eisenkot would usher the Arab parties into power.
In one of several AI-generated videos posted by Netanyahu, Eisenkot was portrayed astride a wooden Trojan horse, with Abbas and left-wing politician Yair Golan inside.
Abbas said Friday that he was coordinating with other Arab leaders on “the prospects for forming a government to replace the one led by Netanyahu.”

Eisenkot’s anti-Netanyahu bloc contains a broad array of ideologies and views on the issue, ranging from Golan, who has publicly advocated for a deal with the Arab parties, to Avigdor Lieberman of the right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu party, who continues to oppose working with them.
With that much friction, a stalemate and more elections remain a real possibility.

Fawaz Gerges, a professor of international relations at the London School of Economics, told NBC News that Israel still appears stuck, adding that Eisenkot’s conditions for the Arab parties are effectively asking them to “forsake their identity.”
“I don’t think we will see the opposition led by Eisenkot forming a government in Israel,” he said. “So what we have now is a deadlock.”
For the major Israeli parties, it is a choice “between Israel as a democratic state or Israel as a Zionist exclusive society,” he said.
But Yossi Mekelberg, a senior consulting fellow with the Middle East and North Africa Program at U.K. think tank Chatham House, sees flexibility that could yield a breakthrough.
Parties “make all these promises before the election, and it is obvious that you break at least some of them after the election,” he said.

articles.title: Transport minister forced to take back seat at his own press conference
articles.author: Stephanie Richards

paras.en: That was the intervention from the South Australian Treasurer, just four minutes after journalists began questioning the under-fire Transport Minister Joe Szakacs over a mounting controversy.

Mr Szakacs had not faced the press pack in more than a week, amid a series of damaging revelations over the state's biggest and most expensive road infrastructure project — the $15.4 billion Torrens to Darlington build.

The rather convoluted "who knew what when and how could this have ever been allowed to happen" saga centres on an alleged attempt from an outlaw gang member to muscle in on a labour hire company that had won a contract on the project.

By Tuesday afternoon, the story had made headlines for longer than a fortnight (much to the chagrin of the tight-shipped Malinauskas government), yet it showed no signs of slowing down, thanks to news breaking overnight that the labour hire company's contract had been terminated.
It is pertinent to note the somewhat awkward interaction between Mr Szakacs and Treasurer Tom Koutsantonis at the press conference was not spurred by reporters.
On the contrary, it appeared to be a veiled intervention on Mr Koutsantonis's behalf.
In the lead-up to it, Mr Szakacs was asked by an ABC journalist what prompted the termination of the contract.

The minister replied saying the labour hire firm had been "directed off site" for failing to advise the Torrens to Darlington Alliance of civil litigation "where one alleged shareholder was suing another alleged party who was a known bikie".
"I just want to be clear on this though, because I think …" the ABC journalist started to say, before Mr Koutsantonis quickly interjected from behind, before making his way to the microphones.
From the outset, Mr Szakacs, as both transport and infrastructure minister, was the most qualified person in the room to respond to the journalist's line of questioning.

Yet the fact his veteran colleague — the so-called "Labor Lion" and former infrastructure and transport minister — felt it necessary to take over the prickly task is a telling sign of the trouble the Malinauskas government currently finds itself in.
Scandal is not a word to which the Malinauskas-led Labor team is accustomed.

In fact, not since the lead-up to the March election, when the party found itself having to defend a questionable decision to release a patient's private email to "background journalists", has it copped such sustained political heat.

Day after day of negative headlines and mounting pressure on a key minister is foreign territory for a government which has spent the past four-and-a-half years with an iron-like grip on South Australian politics.

Mr Szakacs is by no means a "junior" minister (he held various ministerial portfolios throughout the previous term), but being handed the weighty responsibility of overseeing transport and infrastructure at such a critical juncture in the Torrens to Darlington build was always going to be a step up.

Whether it is a step he has been able to make is now an open question — with the premier and his senior lieutenants being grilled on multiple occasions in the past fortnight about whether it's time for Mr Szakacs to fall on his sword, over a scandal that is not going away.
That question was one Mr Szakacs faced when he eventually made his way back to the journalists' microphones at Tuesday's press conference, where he was pressed on whether his role was tenable.
"My job is to continue delivering this nation-building, state-building project," he replied, as Mr Koutsantonis nodded behind him.
"My job is to deliver it on time and on budget.
"My job is to ensure there are 5,500 South Australians who are working today because of this project.
"That is my sole focus and I am extremely dedicated and will remain so".
But in the party room, Mr Szakacs has a much more nuanced job — to protect the government, and in particular Premier Peter Malinauskas, from scandal.
And whether he is currently achieving that is very much up for debate.

articles.title: Accused to face murder trial after defence argues dead man stabbed himself
articles.author: Emma Masters

paras.en: A man charged with the stabbing murder of his cousin in Alice Springs last year has been committed to stand trial after arguing the 27-year-old may have stabbed himself.
Local Court Judge John McBride said it would be up to a jury to decide whether a fatal stab wound to the dead man's heart was caused by his cousin Kaine Fisher.
Mr Fisher is due to face the Supreme Court on December 2.
A man accused of fatally stabbing his cousin in the Alice Springs CBD last year has been committed to stand trial in the Northern Territory Supreme Court for his alleged murder.

Kaine Fisher, 23, faced the Alice Springs Local Court this week accused of stabbing the 27-year-old man — referred to in court as Kumanjayi Gibson for cultural reasons — on Gregory Terrace on May 15 last year.
Mr Gibson died in palliative care in Alice Springs less than two months later.
Around a dozen supporters and family members sat quietly in the small courtroom while Judge John McBride outlined the evidence presented during the committal hearing.
"Both the accused and Kumanjayi come from the same community of Nyirripi, about 440 kilometres north-west of Alice Springs," he said.
"Cousins to each other, Kumanjayi's mother is the elder sister of the accused's mother."

The court heard the two men travelled to Alice Springs with extended family and had been drinking at bars that afternoon, but Mr Gibson had not been allowed into the last venue before the incident occurred.
Judge McBride said CCTV footage showed the group leaving the premises around 5pm and then Mr Gibson running towards Mr Fisher on Gregory Terrace.
"Upon reaching the corner of Todd Street and Gregory Terrace, Kumajayi can be seen armed with two steak knives, one in each hand, chasing after the accused," he said.
"Various movements and moments in a rapidly evolving sequence of interactions between different individuals were captured by CCTV cameras and on personal device videos."

The court heard two other relatives became involved, including Poulson Fisher, who moved to stand between Mr Gibson and the accused, and Leroy Gibson, who intervened to wrestle the knives from the 27-year-old.
Judge McBride said it "can be seen on the footage the accused, on reaching Mr Gibson, applied force to his chest on two occasions in quick succession".
Defence lawyer Beth Wild previously told the court there was evidence Mr Gibson had a history of self-harm, including scarring on his chest.
Ms Wild said his aunt had provided a statement saying "that is what he does, that he stabs himself when upset or doesn't get what he wants".

But the Crown argued Mr Fisher was holding an edged weapon when he ran at Mr Gibson and struck him in the chest and in committing Mr Fisher to trial, Judge McBride said it would be a matter for a jury to decide.
"It ended up with Leroy Gibson getting hold of one of the knives and with the other one suggested to fall across the footpath towards the kerb," Judge McBride said.
"At no time prior to this does the available CCTV footage show Kumanjayi making any observable movement with either of the knives consistent with a self-harm stabbing.
"After Kumanjayi gets up from where he had been pushed down by the accused, for a moment he remains standing on the footpath, remonstrating.
"He then removes his singlet, he takes a few steps, before drawing attention to the blood which was coming out of the visible wound to his chest.
"Kumanjayi then stumbles backwards towards the roadside next to the curb and crumples to the ground."

The court heard the 27-year-old received first aid from bystanders, including an off-duty doctor and nurse, before paramedics arrived to provide emergency care and take him to the Alice Springs Hospital.

Judge McBride said the autopsy showed a single stab wound that pierced Mr Gibson's heart and a doctor found the "cause of death can be attributed to complications following the stab wound to the heart".

He said it would be up to the jury to say whether Mr Fisher was holding an edged weapon when he struck Mr Gibson or if "prior to his collapse, Kumanjayi self-harmed, as it was said he was prone to do, only this time fatally".
Mr Fisher was refused bail and is due to face the Supreme Court on December 2.

articles.title: Councillor resigns after probe into domestic violence comment
articles.author: Nakita Jager

paras.en: Noel Selby resigns from Kempsey Shire Council after Facebook comment backlash
Noel Selby has resigned from Kempsey Shire Council after he was found to have made an offensive comment to a woman on Facebook.
Councillors unanimously called for his resignation last month, but Mr Selby maintained his account had been hacked.
The council is expected to hold a by-election in the next three months.

articles.title: Dozens still missing in Russian, guided-bomb attack that killed more than 30 in southern Ukraine

paras.en: Dozens still missing in Russian, guided-bomb attack that killed more than 30 in southern Ukraine
Kremlin says talks with Ukraine, U.S. will take place Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi
Rescuers in southern Ukraine continued an intense search for survivors Tuesday at a bombed-out aid facility and shelter where at least 31 people were killed and dozens were still missing.

Teams of emergency workers and volunteers picked through debris at the cratered blast site in Komyshuvakha, a village in Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia region, where bodies were pulled from the rubble and carried away in white plastic sheeting. More than 45 residents are still missing.

"The scale of the tragedy is terrifying," Mykhailo Semikin, acting head of the region's military administration, wrote in an online post. "This is one of the worst tragedies in terms of the number of civilian victims in our region since the start of the full-scale war."
Three days of mourning were declared in Zaporizhzhia, where Russian bunker-busting bombs, some filled with nearly 1.5 tonnes of explosives, were used in Monday's attack.
The dead included four police officers and two rescue workers, Semikin said Tuesday. At least five people were hurt.

Russia launched 289 attack drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles across nine regions, triggering emergency power cuts, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an online post that noted the barrage coincided with U.S. elections.

"The Russians think America won't notice this signal of theirs," Zelenskyy said. "But we need to notice and stop such terror. We need to help Ukraine defend its skies; otherwise, Russia will never stop its missile strikes."
Amid the attacks, diplomatic efforts aimed at ending the nearly five-year war are taking place.

Zelenskyy was in Berlin on Tuesday to meet with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has made clear he intends to show his support for the Ukrainian leader a week before U.S.-brokered Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations resume.

Germany has become Ukraine's largest supporter in its war with Russia since Donald Trump returned to office last year and withdrew U.S. financial support. Washington still provides intelligence to Ukraine and allows other countries to buy U.S. weapons on Kyiv's behalf.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy are shown arriving for a joint news conference in Berlin on Tuesday. (Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters)
Russia and Ukraine will head to Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates on Nov. 10-11 for talks that include U.S. officials, it was confirmed Tuesday.
Zelenskyy said from Berlin that security guarantees, an "energy ceasefire" and a truce in the Black Sea to guarantee food exports will be discussed in Abu Dhabi.
The Kremlin said that Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin, will serve as Moscow's chief negotiator at the talks.
- Prime Minister says Russia will not be allowed to compete at 2026 world juniors in Alberta
- Analysis Trump's increasing support for Russia carries existential danger for Canada

Previous attempts by Turkey to mediate an end to the war that started with Russia's invasion in February 2022 did not lead to a breakthrough, though the two sides made a number of exchanges of prisoners and war dead.
Ahead of those talks, the European Commission on Wednesday will host a meeting on the war in Ukraine. Representatives of the U.S., Ukraine, NATO and European allies are expected to participate.

White House envoys have talked to both sides in recent weeks as the U.S. looks to mediate a peace deal to end the war, Europe's deadliest conflict since the Second World War. But questions have emerged as to American loyalties in the wake of a diesel deal the U.S. struck with Russia, and antagonistic statements made by Trump regarding Zelenskyy.
Ukraine and Russia both agreed to a six-day ceasefire for humanitarian purposes last week in the southern Ukraine city of Oleshky, in the Kherson region.

Melania Trump, the wife of the U.S. president, helped push for that ceasefire and will host representatives from Ukraine and Russia at the White House on Thursday. It was not immediately clear who would be representing the two countries.

Meanwhile, Moscow kept up its nightly attacks on power plants and energy infrastructure ahead of winter, causing extensive damage and electricity outages as it carried out 20 strikes in 10 regions overnight, Ukraine's Energy Ministry said.
In the northeast region of Kharkiv, a combined Russian missile and drone attack wounded at least 62 people, local authorities said.

A strike damaged a medical facility in the Nemyshlianskyi district, shattered windows in four apartment buildings and damaged cars. More than 200 patients were transferred to other medical facilities, head of the regional military administration Oleh Syniehubov said.
In the Dnipro area, rescuers pulled a woman alive from the rubble Tuesday morning, after a Russian attack killed one person and wounded 17, local authorities said.
The attack damaged an outpatient clinic and a hospital. Patients were transferred to other hospitals, said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of that regional military administration.
- Video Ukraine, Russia both say they were hit by cyberattacks
- Ukraine says its military did not violate Starlink terms, disputing Elon Musk claim
Russia's Defence Ministry said Tuesday that it had shot down 856 Ukrainian drones overnight. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 493 drones were fired toward the Russian capital.

A Ukrainian drone attack wounded two employees at an oil refinery in the Russian city of Yaroslavl, regional Gov. Mikhail Yevrayev said Tuesday. He added that there was damage to the refinery's infrastructure due to a fire that erupted from an attack involving 124 drones.
The Slavneft Yaroslavnefteorgsintez (YANOS) oil refinery, which Ukraine has struck at least twice before, is located some 250 kilometres northeast of Moscow.
Rolling blackouts have been instituted in the south, west and east of Russian-occupied Crimea following attacks on energy infrastructure, Moscow-installed officials said Tuesday.

articles.title: Trump claims U.S. will halt $4B US funding to Israel at end of 2026, as midterms underway

paras.en: Trump claims U.S. will halt $4B US funding to Israel at end of 2026, as midterms underway
No immediate comment from Netanyahu's office on U.S. president's remarks

U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday said he made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Washington would stop $4 billion US in annual funding to Israel after this year, but will still sell weapons to its close Middle East ally.

In a surprise announcement as U.S. voters headed to the polls for midterm elections that will decide whether Trump's Republicans will lose control of Congress, Trump cast the move as partly meant to take away a "bad talking point" he said left-wing Democrats had used against Republicans over support for military assistance to Israel.

Trump did not provide details or explain how the funding would be halted at the end of the year, given that the memorandum of understanding that provides $3.8 billion in U.S. military aid to Israel each year does not expire until September 2028.

But he seemed to acknowledge that aid to Israel, no longer the solid source of bipartisan consensus it had been for decades, had become a political liability for him among some voters. Analysts suggested his declaration was timed as an Election Day ploy.
Discussions have been under way on how Washington's assistance to Israel would evolve beyond 2028, and Netanyahu had already said he expects U.S. aid to wind down over time.
- A new progressive wave is exposing the Democratic rift over Israel — just the way Republicans want it
- Lack of big-name Democratic candidates at pro-Israel conference confirms for some voters the party has changed

Trump, however, appeared to signal that his mind was made up about what would mark a significant shift in U.S.-Israel relations, even as the two countries remain in conflict with Iran more than eight months after jointly attacking the Islamic Republic.

Trump told Fox News' Fox & Friends program that Israel no longer needed the funding and that some Democrats and left-wing politicians were using the financial support to criticize Republicans. Opinion polls show that the U.S. public's overall support for Israel has declined mostly due to the Gaza war.

"Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion [US] a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping," Trump said. "We've already agreed that by the end of this year we won't be paying Israel. Now, we'll help Israel if they need it."

Israel's future leadership is uncertain after an Oct. 27 election in which Netanyahu — who has allied himself tightly with the U.S. Republicans — lost his governing majority but denied his opponents a clear path to unseat him. The election results paved the way for what are expected to be protracted negotiations over a new government.
Neither the White House nor Netanyahu's office responded to Reuters' requests for comment.

But Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the rival bloc seeking to oust Netanyahu, wrote on X: "The fact that the security establishment, along with Israeli citizens, is learning about a change in the strategic relationship framework through the media highlights just how much Benjamin Netanyahu's conduct poses a genuine danger. We can no longer rely on him and must replace him."
U.S. public support for Israel has fallen, particularly among Democrats, since Israel's harsh response in Gaza to the deadly Hamas-led cross-border attack in October 2023.

A Quinnipiac University poll in June found 48 per cent of voters and 66 per cent of Democrats believe the U.S. is too supportive of Israel — up from 16 per cent and 20 per cent, respectively, when the question was first asked in 2017.

Polls and nonpartisan analysts say that Democrats are likely to wrest control of the House of Representatives from Trump's Republican Party in Tuesday's elections. Control of the Senate remains uncertain.
A number of candidates critical of Israel won Democratic primaries over the past year, and even moderate lawmakers have been increasingly willing to challenge long-time U.S. support.

In a key battleground race, Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed is vying to represent Michigan in the Senate. El-Sayed, who would become the first Muslim to serve as a U.S. senator, has opposed unconditional military aid to Israel.

Trump said the left used the U.S. funding as a "signal of unfairness" and that he could not allow that to happen. He specifically mentioned El-Sayed when explaining why he said Washington was stopping the money.
"Because they [Israel] don't need it, and because why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don't need it?" Trump said. "It's a bad talking point."

Some members of Trump's Make America Great Again movement have also become increasingly critical of Israel, accusing it of having misled the president — who campaigned on a promise to avoid foreign interventions — into believing Iran could easily be defeated. Polls show most Americans oppose the war, which has driven up U.S. gasoline prices and pushed down Trump's approval ratings.

"The curious issue is timing," said Jon Alterman of the Center for Strategic and International Studies think-tank in Washington. "Why did President Trump announce it on Election Day? And why did he announce it amidst speculation that a major joint U.S.-Israeli military strike against Iran may be days away?"
- Analysis Young men and right-leaning podcasters helped Trump win in 2024. Both have soured on him
- Netanyahu's party amplifies unproven claims that Arab-led parties have ‘stolen' Israel's election

While some U.S. supporters of Israel urged Trump to reconsider and instead phase out the funding gradually, Rep. Ro Khanna, a progressive Democrat from California, said on X that "Zero aid Israel" would be part of his party's agenda if it wins congressional control.
Meanwhile, Republican Rep. Don Bacon told CNN: "What I really had heartburn about is the Israelis didn't know about it."
Congress passed a law in 2020 authorizing the funding for Israel, but the Senate and House must still pass appropriations bills every year to distribute and release the funds.

Netanyahu said in an interview with an Israeli television channel in October: "If you think we're going to continue receiving what I secured twice, and that's tens of billions of dollars in American aid for the defence budget, prepare yourselves and get used to the fact that it won't happen, because America has changed."

In anticipation of the possible reduction of U.S. financial support in the coming years, the House this past summer passed a defence bill provision that would deepen U.S.-Israeli military technology ties.

The provision of the 2027 National Defence Authorization Act, known as Section 219, envisions a much deeper defence co-operation between the two countries. Dozens of NGOs have called the idea "exceptionally dangerous" and urged U.S. lawmakers to scrap it.

articles.title: Parts of small plane that crashed in South Florida found as far as 6 km from where it came down

paras.en: Parts of small plane that crashed in South Florida found as far as 6 km from where it came down
NTSB confirms parts of jet's tail likely fell off aircraft before crashing
Investigators have found part of the tail of the jet that crashed in South Florida over the weekend more than a kilometre from the crater caused when the aircraft made impact.

National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said during a news conference Tuesday that the discovery of tail parts broken into three pieces confirms the plane was breaking apart before it hit the ground.
Three pieces of the tail's elevator were found over a range of about two to six kilometres from the crater site.
"It seems implausible that it would have been a result of the impact," he said. "It would have separated before the impact."

Without the tail intact, the plane wouldn't have been able to pull up from its nosedive, he said. But Chapman added he's not sure it would have been effective even if it was intact because of the extreme speed of the aircraft's descent.

"The function of the elevator is to control the pitch up and down," he said. "At those speeds I don't know that it would've been effective even if it had still been attached to the aircraft, but knowing that it was lost is a very important piece of evidence in terms of pointing us towards other things to investigate."

The co-pilot, Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, told air traffic controllers minutes before the crash that ice was accumulating on the plane and that severe turbulence had thrown it up and down by more than 210 metres.
Investigators had to remove a utility pole from the area of the crater before they could access the plane wreckage. (Rebecca Blackwell/The Associated Press)

The the Bahamas-bound Learjet 60 hit bad weather Sunday and slammed into the ground about 11 kilometres southwest of Palm Beach. The plane hit the ground with enough force to create a crater before bursting into flames. The impact scattered plane fragments over a large area.
Chapman said significant progress has been made in terms of being able to get access to the crater, where he said investigators expect to find "critical airplane components."

"With the force of that impact, even the elements of the aircraft that are in the crater are going to be very likely in smaller pieces," he said. "So we don't know exactly what all we have yet, but that's part of the investigation.... It's a big puzzle to try to put together."

The plane took off from Austin, Texas. The victims included technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife, Helen Sharp, and their two young children, relatives said. The family's nanny was also with them.
Filgueiras' stepfather, Thiago Corteleti, told the New York Post that she texted her boyfriend about 10 minutes before the crash, telling him, "I've got turbulence, I've got ice."

The texts were reportedly sent before the situation became critical. In the last two minutes of the flight, Filgueiras shifted from calmly communicating with air traffic controllers to calling out terrifying updates as the plane plummeted.

The Federal Aviation Administration prohibits commercial airline pilots from using cellphones at any point during a flight. The rules aren't as strict for pilots of charter flights; they are not supposed to use cellphones during critical phases of flight, such as takeoffs and landings, but are allowed while cruising at altitude unless their company or pilot in command specifically bans it.

Chapman said Monday that weather would be a key focus of the investigation. A preliminary report describing what happened will be released in about a month, but it will likely take more than a year to determine the cause of the crash.

articles.title: Multiple flights to European airports targeted by bomb threats

paras.en: Polish authorities said they carried out inspections of two passenger planes targeted by bomb threats on Tuesday but did not find any explosives, in a string of bomb threats that hit several European airports.
A bomb alert forced a LOT flight from London's Heathrow to make an unscheduled landing at Warsaw-Modlin airport, prompting the airport to shut down. Operations resumed around midday.

"The passengers were evacuated and the plane underwent security checks. Nothing was found," airport spokesman Adam Szablowski told the French AFP news agency. "The airport has been reopened and is operating normally."
A SAS Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen also received a bomb threat before landing safely at Warsaw's central Chopin airport, where it underwent a security inspection.
No explosives were found on either plane. It was not immediately clear whether the threats were linked.
Flights bound for Spain, Bulgaria also targeted
Also on Tuesday, a Ryanair flight from Manchester, UK, to Murcia, Spain, was hit by a bomb threat. It landed safely and underwent checks after all the passengers had disembarked.
The Spanish government's delegate in the region of Murcia, Francisco Lucas, confirmed on X that police "ruled out the presence of explosives on the plane."
"The International Airport of the Region of Murcia resumes its activity normally. Thanks to the emergency teams that have participated in the operation," he said.

And in the fourth such incident, the Reuters news agency reported that another flight traveling from Israel landed in the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, on Tuesday after a bomb threat was received via email. Counter-terrorism units were checking the plane for possible explosive devices, BTA news agency quoted Interior Minister Secretary General Lyubomir Nikolov as saying.

Later, two more bomb threats also targeted Ryanair flights from Lisbon and Dublin to Rome’s Fiumicino airport, according to Italian media. Air Force jets were deployed as a result. Both threats turned out to be false alarms.
The six threats on Tuesday come after a WizzAir flight from London to Sofia was redirected to the Hungarian capital, Budapest, on Monday after it received a bomb threat mid-air.
Similar such incidents have been reported across different European airports in recent weeks, with alerts later turning out to be false.

articles.title: Yemen: Houthi clashes near Taiz leave residents in a 'state of panic'

paras.en: Four months into the fighting in Yemen between the Iran-backed Houthi movement and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, clashes are concentrated around Taiz in the country's southwest. Yemeni authorities have warned civilians of sniper fire from surrounding hillsides. Houthi forces have also largely blocked the delivery of goods to Taiz, which is under the control of government forces.

Taiz is Yemen's third-largest city, with a population of around 1 million people. However, fighting has displaced around 134,000 people in the Taiz governorate region, accordingto the International Organization for Migration. The governorate accounts for almost half of the more than 319,000 people displaced across western Yemen, the organization said on November 1, 2026.

"The Houthis have blocked fuel, water and medical supplies, basically all things required for hospitals to function properly," Niku Jafarnia, Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, told DW. "Even those who can reach hospitals may not be receiving the care they need," she said, adding that it has had a devastating impact on people's health, particularly those with chronic illnesses.
Ammar, a 45-year-old photographer in Taiz, told DW on Monday that he sees people in a "state of panic" and yet he feels that "the determination not to submit to the Houthis is very strong."

Afnan, the mother of a schoolchild in Taiz, told DW that "neighbors share the little food they have and help each other and many people in Taiz refuse to flee." She and the other residents who spoke to DW asked that their full names not be published, fearing reprisals.

Hanan, a 30-year-old mother of three, said that prices have skyrocketed while there is almost no petrol, cooking gas or drinking water left in the city. "This increases the mental load on people who are already scared by hearing the clashes of the fighting day and night," she said. Despite this, she numbers among those who have decided to stay.

Meanwhile, Nabil Shamsan, the governor of Taiz, told DW that negotiations are underway to bring food, fuel and water back to the city. While it remains to be seen when and under what conditions this might happen, international aid organizations remain extremely concerned.

"Fighting and insecurity around Taiz is making it unsafe for civilians to move freely and also for our staff to deliver aid," said Alison Bottomley, an advocacy adviser with the Norwegian Refugee Council in Yemen. "This is preventing us from reaching the 7,000 people we are supporting with emergency tents, blankets and educational activities for displaced children," she told DW, calling on both factions to allow "civilians and humanitarian workers to move safely."

During the previous Yemen conflict, which began in 2014 and largely ended with a UN-brokered truce in 2022, Ansar Allah, the formal name of the Houthi group, had already laid siege to Taiz in 2015 and 2016. That siege brought the population close to famine and caused a humanitarian crisis, but the Houthis never captured the city.

In turn, Taiz, as a bastion of resistance, represents something the Houthis have struggled to subdue for more than a decade, Hisham Al-Omeisy, a senior Yemeni adviser with UK-based advisory firm Coral Core Consultants, told DW. "The city symbolizes a deeply rooted tradition of political pluralism, civic resistance and rejection of the Houthi model of rule," he said, adding that the city's continued resistance is both a military obstacle and a political challenge to the Houthis' claim that their authority across Yemen is inevitable.
