articles.title: Multiple bankruptcies surround businessman at centre of T2D dispute
articles.author: Thomas Kelsall and Kathryn Bermingham

paras.en: The businessman claiming ownership of a company that won a now-cancelled contract on the $15.4 billion Torrens to Darlington project has been bankrupt four times.
He was also previously in a dispute with the tax office over more than $2 million in "unreported and unexplained income" used to finance gambling losses.
The lead contractors of the South Road project will appear before a parliamentary committee later this month.

The businessman claiming ownership of a labour hire firm that won a now-cancelled contract on the $15.4 billion Torrens to Darlington project has been bankrupt four times, including when the company won the public tender.

Robert Mark Cammarano was also previously in a dispute with the tax office over whether more than $2 million used to fund gambling losses at Crown Casino was required to be declared as taxable income, the ABC can reveal.

Mr Cammarano, 55, is suing in the Supreme Court, claiming beneficial ownership of all 100 shares in labour hire company Career Boss Australia, which in mid-2025 won a contract to supply workers to the Torrens to Darlington (T2D) project.
The South Australian government said Mr Cammarano "wasn't a shareholder" when the contract was awarded. He was also not listed as a company director.
Mr Cammarano alleges in his statement of claim that bikie Jamie Brown "coerced the transfer" of shares in the company by making "express threats of physical harm".
Brown is yet to file a defence but has reportedly said he has "never threatened any shareholder and allegations to the contrary are simply false".
Other respondents to the case have reportedly indicated they will dispute Mr Cammarano's ownership claims to the company.
The Malinauskas government asked the T2D Alliance to suspend its contract with Career Boss Australia when Mr Cammarano's court action was reported in the media on October 18.

On Monday, the T2D Alliance, led by contractor John Holland, cancelled the Career Boss contract entirely, although a court heard the labour hire company was still owed around $2 million for work performed.
Mr Cammarano has been declared and discharged from bankruptcy on four separate occasions, according to Australian Financial Security Authority records.
The declarations were made in 2000, 2007, 2016 and 2023.
All four bankruptcies were by debtors petition, meaning Mr Cammarano applied to make himself bankrupt.
He was not discharged from the latest bankruptcy until February 23, 2026, meaning he was a declared bankrupt when Career Boss Australia was awarded the T2D labour hire contract last year.
Mr Cammarano was not listed as a Career Boss director when the contract was awarded, according to ASIC records.

Asked whether the state government should have known about the past bankruptcies before the contract was awarded, Mr Cammarano's lawyer, Scott Jelbert, told the ABC: "I don't think that they should have known."
"He wasn't representing himself as the party they were contracting with," he said, adding that Mr Cammarano's interests were managed through a trust with his family "as the beneficiary".
Mr Jelbert did, however, say that Mr Cammarano was not "hiding in the shadows" when Career Boss was preparing to tender for work on the South Road project.
"I think they knew of him," Mr Jelbert said of the T2D Alliance's knowledge of Mr Cammarano, adding "he was a bankrupt and that happens".
"He was up-front about his involvement with the company, for sure," he said.
The ABC contacted John Holland but the company declined to comment.
Mr Jelbert said one of his client's bankruptcies came following a dispute with the Australian Tax Office over "unreported and unexplained income".
Mr Cammarano declared a taxable income of $61,405 in 2017–18 and $61,789 in 2018–19, according to an Administrative Appeals Tribunal judgment.
But the ATO amended the assessment based on records supplied by Crown Casino in Melbourne.
"Funds used by [Mr Cammarano] to finance his gambling losses represented funds available to him in some form," the judgment said.
His income was adjusted to nearly $1.5 million in 2017–18 and $963,339 in 2018–19.
Mr Jelbert said the full amounts were not disclosed by Mr Cammarano because he did not count loans as income.
"The ATO found it … asked about it and said that 'we think that they weren't loans, you should have characterised that as income'," he said.
'Good questions' for T2D Alliance, treasurer says

The T2D Alliance has been compelled to appear before parliament's budget and finance committee on November 16, where they are likely to face questions on what due diligence they did on Career Boss before awarding the contract.
Treasurer Tom Koutsantonis was asked on Tuesday whether Mr Cammarano had any meeting with the Alliance before or during the tender process.
"From what I can see, he wasn't a shareholder," Mr Koutsantonis said.
"So, I don't know in what capacity he would have had meetings with the alliance.
"But these are questions that John Holland and [fellow contractor] Bouygues [Construction Australia] are happy to answer, happy to answer in a parliamentary committee.

"These are good questions to put to them because if they have hired someone that they shouldn't have hired, if they have given a contract to someone they shouldn't have given a contract to, then they should terminate those contracts."

articles.title: Airbnb levy needed to 'turbocharge' community housing build, industry says
articles.author: Declan Bowring

paras.en: The peak body for the community housing industry has called for land tax changes and a new levy on short-stay rentals to raise $26 billion towards new community housing builds.
The NSW social housing waiting list has grown to 72,000, which the Community Housing Industry Association NSW (CHIA) boss says is a record.
NSW Housing Minister Rose Jackson says the government is investing $6.6 billion into new social and affordable homes.

A 7.5 per cent levy on short-stay rentals, land tax reform and a rezoning windfall charge are among a suite of recommendations the NSW community housing sector is calling for to boost housing stock and address lengthy housing waiting lists.

The Community Housing Industry Association NSW (CHIA) is pitching to the NSW government to adopt measures they say could raise $26 billion over the next 10 years and provide support for around 50,000 new social and affordable homes by 2050.

Among the proposals analysed by the Labor-aligned McKell Institute is increasing NSW land tax rates from 1.6 per cent to 2 per cent and from 2 per cent to 2.5 per cent for larger landholdings, while also adding a new 2.9 per cent rate for holdings above $50 million.
The changes would still retain the $1.075 million tax-free threshold and the family home exemption and would bring in an estimated $25.9 billion over 10 years.

CHIA NSW is also proposing a 7.5 per cent levy on short-stay rentals like Airbnb and Stayz, similar to the Victorian scheme that came into force last year. The levy is expected to raise $135 million annually.
CHIA NSW CEO Luke Achterstraat said the proposals would help the 72,000 NSW households that remained on the social housing waiting list, which he said was an "all-time record".
"Whilst we acknowledge the government's record $6.6 billion building homes for NSW package, we argue that funding should be turbocharged," Mr Achterstraat said.
"We felt it was important to make a constructive contribution to provide government with options they may consider."
Mr Achterstraat stressed that the proposals were options rather than a full package of reforms.
The peak body also suggested a windfall charge for land value increases after rezoning, which would raise $80 million a year.
Mr Achterstraat said the revenue should be channelled into a long-term funding pool for community housing for future builds.

"We need to move beyond funding cliffs and establish a long-term investment pipeline that gives community housing providers the certainty to keep building homes year after year,” Mr Achterstraat said.
CHIA NSW will present the commissioned research at an event in the NSW parliament today.
Housing Minister Rose Jackson said the Labor government was investing $6.6 billion to deliver tens of thousands of social and affordable homes.
"We're building 8,400 new public homes that will be owned by the people of NSW and remain part of the public housing system for generations," Ms Jackson said.
"A long-term pipeline of social and affordable housing is essential to tackling the housing crisis.
"We welcome constructive ideas from across the sector. Our focus is on getting more homes built and more people housed."

Shadow Housing Minister Chris Rath said the government was not using the $6.6 billion funding package fast enough and was 40 per cent behind on their National Housing Accord target of 377,000 new homes by 2029.
"We need to be building more of everything, everywhere, all at once, and community housing is a key part of that housing mix,"
"The social housing waitlist has increased from 55,000 to 72,000 under their watch. This is a massive failure."
Mr Rath said the coalition planned to build 12,000 new homes to replace Long Bay Correctional Complex, 30 per cent of which would be social and affordable housing.

NSW Greens housing spokesperson Jenny Leong said the government needed to look at rent controls to address the growing social housing waiting list. Her party has called for a rent freeze and then a 2 per cent annual cap on rent increases.
"We need investment in public housing, we need government support for genuinely affordable community housing, we need a crackdown on those seeking to profit from the housing crisis," Ms Leong said.
Short-term rental industry says levy not the answer

Australia and New Zealand Short Term Rental Association (ASTRA) chair Yoav Tourel said short-term accommodation was also used by people for reasons other than holidays, such as travel for medical treatment, interim accommodation during property repairs, and escaping domestic violence.

"ASTRA absolutely recognises the seriousness of Australia's housing affordability crisis and supports measures that genuinely increase social, affordable and long-term housing supply," Mr Tourel said.
"Our concern is whether a blanket 7.5 per cent levy on short-term accommodation is the most effective way to achieve that.
"A levy may raise revenue for housing, but raising revenue and delivering additional homes are two different outcomes."
Ms Jackson said the government was reviewing the short-term rental accommodation framework and would provide an update "in due course".
The current framework provides a government-run register of short-term rentals and a 180-day cap in parts of Greater Sydney, the Northern Rivers and Hunter regions.
Ms Leong said a levy was a distraction from solutions such as bans or caps set by local councils.
"Levies don't work to limit short-term rentals, and any money they raise is a drop in the ocean compared to the thousands of homes being lost to investor Airbnbs," Ms Leong said.

articles.title: NSW Liberals hit with MP exodus amid surge in popularity for One Nation
articles.author: Alexander Lewis

paras.en: On Monday morning, New South Wales Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane oozed optimism.
"Watch this space, because I am getting more confident that we will be in government next year," she told 2GB's Ben Fordham.
"You'll be leading a government?" Fordham asked.
But the actions of some of her most experienced colleagues suggest they do not share that confidence, as the Coalition polls behind Labor and a surging One Nation.
On Tuesday, Mark Coure became the third Liberal frontbencher in less than three months to announce their retirement from parliament.
The shadow roads and south west Sydney minister said he would not run again for his southern Sydney seat of Oatley at the March election.
In September, two other members of shadow cabinet, Alister Henskens and James Griffin, announced their own departures from parliament.
So far, six Liberal MPs are not recontesting their seats, including backbenchers Mark Taylor, Ray Williams, and Tanya Davies.
All but Mr Taylor previously served as government ministers, and the loss of decades of experience is unhelpful to Sloane.
Mr Coure's retirement came as a surprise to both sides on Macquarie Street.
He had campaigned fiercely in recent days and weeks, including on proposed train timetable changes, which the government ultimately abandoned.
While he held Oatley by a wafer-thin 0.8 per cent against Labor, it always had been marginal for the veteran MP.
"I bucked the trend every election," Mr Coure told ABC Radio Sydney on Tuesday.
"I wasn't supposed to win the first time or the second time. I wasn't supposed to win the third or fourth time either. But here I am today 15 years later."
The 48-year-old denied that political risk was a factor in his decision, saying he wished to spend more time with his two young sons.
But he also said this: "To walk out undefeated is a feather in my cap."
The Liberals are unlikely to lose Oatley to One Nation, but the orange wave may help deliver it to Labor, thanks to optional preferential voting.
Unlike federal elections, and elections in other mainland states, the New South Wales ballot does not require voters to mark a preference beyond a '1' vote.
As former ABC election analyst Antony Green has pointed out, a switch of Liberal support to One Nation in seats like Oatley places Labor well to win by giving it the highest primary vote.
Labor has its own share of upcoming retirements, with Prospect MP Hugh McDermott, Wyong MP David Harris, and Wallsend MP Sonia Hornery all bowing out at the end of this term.
While Wallsend looks very safe for Labor on paper, with a 31.8 per cent margin, the party is worried the Hunter electorate could fall to One Nation.
Last week, Premier Chris Minns effectively wrote off the Coalition.
"By any poll, by any measure, [One Nation leader] Mike Newman will either be the premier or the opposition leader after the 13th of March," Minns told 2GB.
Mr Newman is the only lower house candidate One Nation has announced to date.
"We're in the thick of recruiting for all remaining 92 seats including Wallsend," Mr Newman told the ABC.
He said there were 900 candidates to process.
There is still a pathway for the Coalition to form government if both sides lose enough seats to One Nation, and One Nation fails to gain a majority.
If none can get there on its own, it will need to make a deal with another, and it seems unlikely One Nation would side with Labor.
Sloane alluded to that on Monday as she talked up the Coalition's chances of entering government next year.
"If it relies on the support of the crossbench, so be it. But everywhere I go, people are upset with Labor," Ms Sloane said.
But that prospect appears not to have been enough to convince at least some of her soon-to-be former colleagues to risk another four years in opposition.

articles.title: String of bomb threats on flights, cruise ship disrupt travel across Europe

paras.en: String of bomb threats on flights, cruise ship disrupt travel across Europe
No explosives found after security sweep on several flights, officials say
At least seven flights and a cruise ship in Europe received bomb threats on Tuesday, causing disruption at airports although no devices were discovered.

At least two flights to Warsaw, two to Sofia, two to Rome and one to Murcia airport in Spain were subjected to the threats on Tuesday, and another flight to Sofia had been threatened a day earlier. An airport in Warsaw was briefly shut and the Italian air force accompanied one of the flights to Rome while an Israel-bound cruise ship was searched for bombs in Greece.
There was no claim of responsibility and officials did not attribute blame. None of the affected airlines responded to Reuters's requests for comment.
Rhys Jones, Analysis Output Manager at aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions, said that seven confirmed bomb threats in a single day impacting flights was exceptional.
"The lack of clear target state, airline, or route indicates that general disruption to aviation operations is the aim," Jones told Reuters.

In the Bulgarian capital of Sofia, a plane flying from Israel landed after a bomb threat was received by email. Counterterrorism units were checking the plane for possible explosive devices, BTA news agency quoted Interior Ministry Secretary General Lyubomir Nikolov as saying.

Bulgaria’s Transport Ministry said bomb threats were made against two planes travelling from Bergamo and Dublin to Sofia on Tuesday. Both landed safely and no explosive devices were found on inspection.
The Bergamo flight was operated by Wizz Air and was carrying 176 passengers, the statement said. The Dublin flight, operated by Ryanair, had 185 passengers on board.
A day earlier, a Wizz Air flight from London to Sofia was diverted to Budapest airport after receiving a bomb threat, Hungarian Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said in a Facebook post.
Last month, a flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna made an emergency landing in Bulgaria following a bomb threat.
Parts of an airport in Murcia, in southeastern Spain, were cordoned off on Tuesday after a bomb threat was reported on a Ryanair flight from Manchester.
But officials said the report proved to be a hoax, and the airport resumed normal operations after authorities found no explosives on board.

A screengrab from a video shows a police officer removing baggage from a Ryanair airplane on Tuesday, after Ryanair's operations centre reported a bomb threat received during the flight from Manchester to Murcia, according to Guardia Civil, in Murcia, Spain. (Forta/Reuters)

A Ryanair flight from Lisbon landed at Rome's Fiumicino airport Tuesday morning after receipt of an email reporting a bomb was on board, according to information provided by a Fiumicino official with knowledge of the events.
Police bomb disposal experts carried out security checks of passengers, crew and baggage, and found no explosives.
Another email reported a bomb on another Ryanair flight to Rome, bound from Dublin.

Italy's air force escorted that plane to Fiumicino and the same ground security procedures were carried out, with no explosives found, the official said. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak publicly.

In Poland, meanwhile, a morning flight by Polish airline LOT from London's Heathrow airport to Warsaw's main Chopin airport was diverted to the Polish capital's Modlin airport after a bomb threat, Polish press agency PAP reported. The Modlin airport was closed temporarily.

LOT later said that the search of the aircraft diverted to Modlin had been completed and that "nothing was found on the aircraft." Passengers on the flight from London to Warsaw, the airline reported, were undergoing border control and, after passing through, would be transported to Chopin Airport by coach, PAP reported.
The Modlin airport later posted a statement saying that there was no real threat and the airport had resumed normal operations. It did not give any further details on the nature of the threats.

Chopin Airport also received information about a potentially dangerous item on board a Scandinavian Airlines, or SAS, flight from Copenhagen to Chopin airport, PAP reported. Piotr Rudzki, the acting director of the Warsaw airport's communications office, told the news agency that standard safety procedures were immediately implemented following the information and one of the airport's runways was closed.
"The passengers disembarked, the plane landed normally; it was not an emergency landing," SAS spokesperson Alexandra Lindgren Kaokju told PAP.
She added that the carrier is currently focusing on providing care to passengers and crew, and the matter has been referred to the Polish police.

The bomb threats came a day after a Wizz Air flight that departed Luton airport, near London, was forced to make an emergency landing in Hungary after a bomb threat was received while the plane was in the air.

Hungary's defence minister said in his Facebook post on Monday that a Gripen fighter jet from the Hungarian Air Force was scrambled to intercept the Wizz Air flight bound for Sofia, Bulgaria, and escorted it safely to the Liszt Ferenc International Airport in Budapest.
Authorities found no threat aboard the aircraft after conducting an inspection of the plane and its passengers, Wizz Air told state news agency MTI.

A fire brigade car is parked by an Israel-bound cruise ship, following a bomb threat which prompted a security operation, after an unknown person claimed an explosive device had been attached to its hull, Greek authorities said, at the port of Syros, Greece on Tuesday. (Giorgos Solaris/Reuters)

An explosives detection dog and a diver searched the Panama-flagged Crown Iris cruise ship on the Greek island of Syros after an unknown person said an explosive device had been attached to the boat's hull, authorities said.
Initial checks found no explosive device with coast guard specialists expected to carry out further inspections before the ship could resume its voyage.

While no country pointed fingers over the bomb threats, they come as European officials have been blaming both Russia and Iran for what they describe as "hybrid attacks" and acts of sabotage. Moscow and Tehran both deny any such campaign.

This week, unidentified hackers shut down fridges in supermarkets in several European countries. Some experts said hoax bomb threats could be part of a similar pattern of low-cost, deniable disruption efforts.

"From railways to the food infrastructure that you see happening with the fridges being hacked and all kinds of other operations, it does fit the narrative of Russian state actors who want to disturb Europe," said Eric Schouten, the head of aviation security group Dyami.

articles.title: Vivienne Jolie drops dad Brad Pitt's last name, following 3 other siblings
articles.author: Alexandra Mae Jones

paras.en: Vivienne Jolie drops dad Brad Pitt's last name, following 3 other siblings
Vivienne Jolie is the 4th child of Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt to change their last name
Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt's daughter, Vivienne, has officially dropped her father's last name, making her the fourth child of the former celebrity couple to do so.
The 18-year-old will now be known as Vivienne Marcheline Jolie, instead of Vivienne Marcheline Jolie-Pitt, according to documents obtained by CBC News.

She initially filed a petition with the Los Angeles County Superior Court to legally drop her father's last name back in July, shortly after her 18th birthday, with the reason for the change listed as "personal."

Four of the six now-adult children shared by Jolie and Pitt have changed their names, effectively legally distancing themselves from their father amid ongoing tensions in the wake of the couple's 2016 split and ensuing legal battle, which included allegations from Jolie that Pitt had been abusive toward her and the children in a 2016 incident.
Pitt was investigated for child abuse at the time and cleared of all wrongdoing.

Vivienne has been using only her mother's last name for at least two years — she was credited as Vivienne Jolie for her work as a volunteer production assistant on the Broadway show The Outsiders, which her mother co-produced.
- Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt’s daughter Vivienne files to drop Pitt's last name
- Zahara Jolie files to legally drop Brad Pitt's name
Judge Virginia Keeny granted Vivienne's petition during a hearing on Monday at the Los Angeles Superior Court's Stanley Mosk Courthouse.
Angelina Jolie poses with her children, from left, Maddox, Vivienne, Zahara, Shiloh and Knox at the premiere for the film Eternals in Los Angeles on Oct. 18, 2021. (Mario Anzuoni/Reuters)
Vivienne, along with her twin brother, Knox, is the youngest of Pitt and Jolie's children. The others are Maddox, 24; Pax, 22; Zahara, 21; and Shiloh, 20.
Shiloh was the first child to drop the Pitt name in 2024. Zahara and Maddox both filed earlier this year, and had the petitions granted in September.

Jolie and Pitt, once one of the most high-profile couples in Hollywood, married in 2014 after a decade together. Jolie filed for divorce in 2016 and a judge declared them legally single in 2019, but their contentious split wasn't completely settled until 2024.

The divorce filing came after an alleged incident on a plane in 2016, the details of which were outlined in court documents filed in 2022. Jolie alleged in the filings that Pitt had grabbed Jolie, pushed her, and choked one of their children and struck another when they tried to intervene. A representative for Pitt denied the allegations, and the FBI stated it had conducted a review and was not pursuing further investigation.
Brad Pitt attends the European premiere for F1: The Movie in London on June 23, 2025. (Maja Smiejkowska/Reuters)
While Jolie has appeared frequently with the children on red carpets, Pitt has not been seen in public with any of his children for years.

The 62-year-old actor has not publicly addressed the name changes of his children. In an August interview with Esquire, he alluded to it, saying he had briefly experienced suicidal ideation over "family stuff," and "didn't see a way out."

The six children have largely kept out of the spotlight and avoided speaking about their family or relationships with either parent. Earlier this year, Zahara praised mother Jolie, 51, during a mother-daughter brunch for the Pearls of Purpose Foundation in Atlanta, saying their relationship was a "kindred" one.
Angelina Jolie and Zahara Marley Jolie attend the 82nd Golden Globe Awards in Beverly Hills on Jan. 5, 2025. (Daniel Cole/Reuters)
"She's the most selfless, loving and understanding woman, who I get to call my mom," she said.

According to People, she ended the speech by turning and directly addressing Jolie, who was in attendance: "I think back to a quote I saw years ago that said, 'I am a strong woman because a strong woman raised me.' Thank you, Mom."

articles.title: Dancing with the Stars 'shock' as fan favourite sent packing
articles.author: Griffin Jaeger

paras.en: Dancing with the Stars 'shock' as fan favourite sent packing
Fairy tale comes to an end for one of the season’s initial fan favourites
A tale as old as time, a tune as old as song: The fairy tale came to an end for one of the season’s initial fan favourites during Monday night’s Disney-themed episode on Dancing with the Stars.
After wowing the judges to a paso doble to Satisfied from Hamilton, the episode really was the last dance for Save the Last Dance star Julia Stiles and her partner, Ezra Sosa.
The ballroom transformed into the happiest place on Earth as couples were tasked with showcasing the magic of Disney on Broadway.

Guest-judged by Cynthia Erivo, star of the Wicked films, the night brought an enchanted flair to the stage, featuring numbers inspired by Hamilton, Beauty and the Beast, The Little Mermaid, Rapunzel, Aida, Hercules and more.
But despite the magic, as per every week, one couple went home.

"It's been an incredible experience. I pulled things out of myself that I didn't realize were there," Stiles said tearfully after being eliminated. "And Ezra is just an amazing person. I'm going to be sad not to see him every day."

Following the show, Stiles's cast-mates reacted backstage. Speaking with Entertainment Tonight, pro dancer Daniella Karagach called the elimination "gut-wrenching." Reality star Maura Higgins said it was "a shock."
When the cast was first announced, Stiles received a ton of support from fans excited to see the star compete. So fans on social media were quick to voice their reactions to Monday's news.
"In my house Julia Stiles will always be the winner idc," one fan wrote on X. "Good morning julia stiles nation im still pissed about last night," wrote another.
Others, however, weren't so shocked. Especially after last week's guest judge Shirley Ballas gave the pair a 4/10. At the time, Stiles said she was working through a rib injury.
"Sorry not sorry but Julia always gets overscored just because she’s Julia Stiles. Ms. Shirley Ballas just gave her the actual score she deserves," a viewer wrote.
- Dancing with the Stars: Julia Stiles honours Heath Ledger with live tribute
- Julia Stiles had her Save the Last Dance moment on Dancing with the Stars

Stiles’s reliance on nostalgia throughout the season also drew criticism. She performed tributes to her well-known films Save the Last Dance and 10 Things I Hate About You, including a tribute to late castmate Heath Ledger.
"Is this a safe space to say that Julia focusing on nostalgia instead of letting us get to actually know her and her life ended up hurting her votes," another viewer wrote.
Monday night's results mean no worries for the rest of the couples, for now.
Stars still competing for the mirror ball and bringing their A game to the ballroom include Tatyana Ali, Jenna Dewan, Ezra Frech, Amber Glenn, Maura Higgins, Harry Shum Jr. and Connor Wood.
After the first dance of the night, host Julianna Hough announced the couple who topped the scoreboard would be immune from next week's dance-off.

It was a toss-up of two. Both Dewan and partner Val Chmerkovskiy and Shum and partner Jenna Johnson received perfect scores for their routines to Be Our Guest from Beauty and the Beast and Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious from Mary Poppins.
Because of the tie, immunity went to the pair with the highest scores throughout the season. Shum Jr. and Johnson won their way with a total of 236.

The night also featured two team dances, one to We're All in This Together from High School Musical and another to Zoo from Zootopia 2. The final standings were calculated by combining the team scores, partner dance scores and fan votes.
Dancing With The Stars airs Tuesdays on Disney+. This week aired early to avoid overlap with the U.S. midterm elections.

articles.title: Cyprus: From ties with Russia to a strategic alignment with the US

paras.en: In an interview with the Cyprus News Agency on October 4, the new US ambassador to Cyprus, John Breslow, outlined plans to upgrade the Andreas Papandreou Air Base in Paphos to accommodate large US military transport aircraft.
He also announced plans for more frequent visits by US warships to Cypriot ports and an expansion of joint military activities.
But one statement carried particular political weight: his assurance that "the United States will protect Cyprus in the future."
Although the remark does not constitute a formal US security guarantee, it reflects the growing cooperation between the two countries.

For a country that for decades maintained close ties with Moscow, viewed US foreign policy with suspicion and is not a member of NATO, the prospect of an expanded American military presence marks a significant geopolitical shift.
It is perhaps the clearest indication yet of Cyprus's gradual loosening of ties with Russia and its increasingly close strategic alignment with the United States.
The shift is particularly striking given Cyprus's political history.
In the years after it gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1960, the Republic of Cyprus sought to balance its relations between East and West.

Under the leadership of Archbishop Makarios III, the first president of independent Cyprus, the country became a founding member in 1961 of the Non-Aligned Movement, a forum of nations that did not align with either of the two superpowers of the day: the United States and the Soviet Union.
This approach allowed Nicosia to maintain close ties with the Soviet Union without severing its connections to the West.
Even after joining the European Union in 2004, Cyprus maintained strong political, economic and military ties with Moscow.
Relations with the United States, by contrast, remained overshadowed by the Turkish invasion of the island in 1974 and the US's failure to take decisive action against Ankara.
The United States prioritized maintaining its strategic relationship with Turkey, a key NATO ally, over taking a tougher stance against the invasion.

The US position fueled widespread anti-American sentiment in Cyprus, culminating in a violent demonstration outside the embassy in Nicosia on August 19, 1974, during which US Ambassador Roger Davies was shot dead.

Mistrust deepened further in 1987, when the United States imposed an arms embargo on the Republic of Cyprus, officially intended to prevent an arms race on the island and avoid undermining efforts to resolve the Cyprus conflict.

The US arms embargo contributed to the reliance of the Cypriot National Guard (the armed forces of the Republic of Cyprus) on Russia-made weapons systems, strengthening the Kremlin's position as a major military partner.
The response by Cyprus to Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 illustrated the strength of these ties.

The Cypriot government expressed serious reservations about imposing tougher EU sanctions on Russia. Then-Foreign Minister Ioannis Kasoulides warned that such measures could have devastating consequences for the Cypriot economy.
Relations with Moscow deepened further in February 2015, when President Nicos Anastasiades visited the Russian capital and signed a series of agreements with President Vladimir Putin.

These included a naval cooperation memorandum facilitating visits by Russian warships to Cypriot ports. Moscow also agreed to more favorable repayment terms for its €2.5 billion loan to Cyprus in 2011.

Cooperation remained close as recently as October 2021, when then Foreign Minister and current President Nikos Christodoulides signed a Strategic Cooperation Framework for 2022–2024 in Moscow alongside his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov.
The decisive turning point came just four months later, in February 2022, with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Konstantinos Adamides, an associate professor of international relations at the University of Nicosia, told DW that the invasion accelerated a geopolitical shift toward the West that had already begun.
"For the first time, the Republic of Cyprus openly and unequivocally chose to side with the West, despite the economic and political costs of breaking with Moscow," Adamides said.
Nicosia aligned itself with EU sanctions against Russia, despite the Cypriot economy's strong links to Moscow, particularly in services, investment and tourism.
The decision marked a significant departure from Cyprus's traditional foreign policy approach of maintaining a balance between Russia and the West.
Adamides said the government's position on Russia paved the way for closer relations with the United States, particularly in the field of security.
Cyprus, he said, succeeded in convincing Washington that it could serve as a reliable partner in the Eastern Mediterranean.
The rapprochement had already gained an institutional foundation before the war, with a bilateral statement of intent on security cooperation signed in 2018.

Further initiatives followed, including the Cyprus Center for Land, Open-seas and Port Security (CYCLOPS), a US-funded training facility inaugurated in Larnaca in April 2022. The center provides training for security personnel from Cyprus and other countries in the region in areas such as port security, counterterrorism and preventing the trafficking of hazardous materials.
An even more significant development for the Cypriot National Guard came in September 2022, when Washington announced the full suspension of the arms embargo imposed in 1987.

The decision allowed for the export of lethal military equipment to Cyprus, subject to the necessary US approvals. The suspension, which was not permanent and remains subject to periodic renewal, has been renewed until September 30, 2027.
The strategic security reorientation is also significant because Cyprus is not a member of NATO.
The crash landing of an Iranian done on the British military base at Akrotiri in March reignited a debate in Cyprus about whether the country should join NATO.
At the time, Christodoulides said Cyprus was preparing for potential membership at the military, operational and administrative level and would apply to join NATO "even tomorrow if it were possible."
Christodoulides said, however, that joining the alliance was not possible because "the political conditions are not there, taking into account the well-known position of Turkey."
The country's changing strategic orientation is also reflected in the modernization of its armed forces.
After decades of relying heavily on Russian military equipment, Cyprus is seeking to gradually reduce its dependence on Russian-made T-80 tanks and Tor-M1 and Buk air defense systems.
The process accelerated following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, as sanctions against Moscow made it increasingly difficult to secure spare parts and ammunition for Russian weapons systems.

Another important step came in January 2025, when then President Joe Biden authorized Cyprus to participate in US defense procurement programs, including Foreign Military Sales (FMS) and Excess Defense Articles (EDA).
The decision gave Nicosia access to additional mechanisms for acquiring US military equipment, further strengthening defense cooperation between Cyprus and the United States.

articles.title: China and India achieved diplomatic thaw. Now the border is flaring up

paras.en: Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur sounded alarm bells across India by confirming that Indian and Chinese troops had confronted each other at several locations along the de facto border in Arunachal Pradesh state, in India's northeast.
"In the past few days, a situation arose where a face-off happened (with Chinese troops) at various locations in Arunachal and it still continues," he told reporters last month.
"It may be difficult to counter China by conventional means because their PLA and BDR (Border Defense Regiment) have gone way ahead with investment and modernization," he said.
The disputed China-India border runs through a remote mountainous region.
Throughout the decades, clashes along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto border, have repeatedly triggered security crises between the world's two most populous nations.
Ties between Beijing and New Delhi are still affected by the deadly violence in 2020, when both countries accused each other of trying to seize territory.

In June that year, a clash in the Galwan River valley in eastern Ladakh killed 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese troops, according to Indian sources. China later confirmed four of its soldiers died.
Arunachal Pradesh leader Pema Khandu says situation normal

Kapur's remarks have brought renewed attention to the Himalayan frontier. Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Pema Khandu has acknowledged but also downplayed the border transgressions, saying such incidents were not new and the situation along the border was normal.
Khandu acknowledged that the border was not properly demarcated and that China did not recognize the McMahon Line, drawn by the British Empire in 1914, which separates Arunachal Pradesh from Tibet.
It was also not clear if the latest confrontations between the Chinese and Indian troops involved physical violence.

The opposition Congress party criticized Khandu's remarks, and accused the ruling BJP, led by India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi, of "rationalizing" Chinese actions instead of asserting India's position.

"On this there has been a deafening silence from the PM and his establishment," Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said in a post on X, referring to the face-offs confirmed by the border police chief.
Meanwhile, External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal attributed the incidents to Chinese forces changing up their patrol routes.
"As we have noted in the past, the situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns," he said.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun rejected the allegations, saying Chinese troops were conducting "normal patrols" and strictly abiding by bilateral agreements.
The LAC largely separates Indian- and Chinese-controlled territory. However, as forces from both nations patrol territory they regard as their own, they sometimes venture into disputed areas.
"There is a very simple reason — because there is no agreed line between the two," Gautam Bambawale, a former Indian ambassador to China, told DW.

The de-facto border stretches for 3,488 kilometres (2,167 miles) according to India, but China claims it is shorter. The two countries have held 25 rounds of talks between their Special Representatives since 2003, but have yet to reach a boundary settlement.
The dispute is particularly sensitive in Arunachal Pradesh, which China claims as part of southern Tibet.
China building a hydropower dam in Tibet
Aravind Yelery, a China expert at Jawaharlal Nehru University, said the region has become more strategically important to Beijing.
"Both sides patrol a contested LAC, so friction is built into the arrangement," Yelery told DW.

"What is new is China's intensified focus on the eastern sector. Since announcing the 60,000-megawatt Medog hydropower project in Tibet, Beijing has poured infrastructure, troops, engineers and machinery into the area."

He described the LAC as "not a thin line but a deep zone of overlapping claims where patrols inevitably meet." Face-offs will continue, he argued, until diplomacy produces concrete arrangements on the ground.
According to Yelery, the diplomatic pledges made by Indian and Chinese leaders will take time to implement.
"A wide gap separates the leaders' promises from the measures that would prevent a repeat of 2020, namely disengagement and mutual restraint," he added.
What is different about the latest developments?
For India, the immediate concern is whether the recent encounters reflect familiar patrol disputes or a more significant change in Chinese activity along the frontier.
Ashok Kantha, another former Indian ambassador to China, said Chinese transgressions in the eastern sector were not new, but that their location and extent mattered.
"If the Chinese have now made deeper intrusions on our side of the LAC, or established a presence in new areas, or expanded their existing presence, that would be a serious development," he added.
He also pointed to agreements signed by the two countries to maintain peace along the border.

"Any such transgression would be in complete violation of several border-related agreements India and China have signed (1993, 1996, 2005, 2012 and 2013). In these, both sides committed to respect and strictly observe the LAC, and not to alter the status quo."
The Indian government has not publicly provided details of the locations or circumstances of the latest face-offs, making it unclear whether they have changed the situation on the ground.

The renewed encounters come as India and China try to stabilize relations and move past the 2020 clashes. Both Beijing and New Delhi made reconciliatory moves, including restoring some direct flights and easing restrictions on travel and economic exchanges.

The diplomatic reset gathered pace after Narendra Modi and Xi Jinping met at the BRICS summit in Kazan, Russia, in October 2024. They met again at the SCO summit in Tianjin in August 2025 and at the BRICS summit in New Delhi this year.
The boundary dispute, however, remains unresolved.
Alka Acharya, director of the Institute of Chinese Studies in New Delhi, cautioned against drawing conclusions about the latest encounters without more information.
The government has described the incidents as face-offs, she said, but has not indicated that Chinese troops have taken control of Indian territory.

"The question is what is the nature of the so-called 'clashes' … not why the clashes are happening again? Any opinion on this latest kerfuffle would at best be conjecture without any definitive evidence," Acharya told DW.

Border incidents have occurred regularly over the past decade and a half, despite political and diplomatic negotiations. The unresolved dispute, she added, will continue to sustain distrust and constrain the broader relationship.
Whether the latest encounters signal a more serious escalation will depend on details that New Delhi has yet to make public.

articles.title: Why South Africa's local elections matter

paras.en: "We've decided not to vote. At all," Vatiswa Zoya said two days before voters in South Africa cast their ballots for new municipal government leaders. "What is the point? We will still sleep hungry."
These very same frustrations are what will lead 22-year-old Lindokuhle Mbandazayo to the polls, although she has yet to decide where to place her cross.

"When we vote for councilors, we ask them to fix the area," Mbandazayo told DW. "The electricity goes off regularly here. There is also sewage in the streets, and we have to jump over this. There are a lot of things that need to be fixed here."

Both women live in Tembisa, a township in Ekurhuleni, a municipality on the outskirts of Johannesburg, South Africa's largest city. Both express an "embedded frustration" over their living conditions.
Sanusha Naidu, an analyst at the Institute for Global Dialogue, said it was this "embedded frustration" that prompts people to vote.
"Your vote actually puts some of these political parties' feet to the fire, but I think that frustration is also inherently coming from the fact that it's not going to happen overnight," Naidu said.

On Wednesday, South Africans will vote in municipal elections that will determine control of the country's largest cities and test whether the African National Congress (ANC), the leading party in the national government coalition, continues its electoral decline.
Here are five things to know about Wednesday's election.
Many voters will be motivated by whether they can shower or not on election day, as many parts of South Africa experience water supply issues.
In Johannesburg, several neighborhoods have faced water cuts and rationing for weeks as old infrastructure struggles to keep up with supply.

"Every province has an issue. So if we take for example drinking water quality, half of the drinking water systems in South Africa are not fit for drinking," Ferrial Adam, executive director of water rights NGO WaterCAN, told DW at a protest over water cuts in Johannesburg.

"Almost 70% of our wastewater treatment works are in a critical state and spewing sewage into rivers and streams across the country," Adam said. "It is a definite water crisis across South Africa," she added.
In Tshwane, a metropolitan area that includes South Africa's administrative capital, Pretoria, a recent water treatment failure left more than 400 residents sick.

Sanusha Naidu, an analyst at the Institute for Global Dialogue, said that, despite widespread worries about water quality and supply, many candidates have not provided adequate details on their solutions.

"I think their promises have been very transactional," Naidu said. "Their promises are always, you know: 'We're going to bring water to your community. We're going to make sure the taps are flowing. We're going to ensure that we're going to deal with the old infrastructure around water, etc.' But I don't think they've dug deeper in terms of understanding what the budgets say about water access."
Many voters place blame for the state of municipalities on the African National Congress, which has historically held an outright majority in most municipalities.

In 2016 the ANC secured 53.91% of the overall vote and had an outright majority in 161 of 213 councils. In 2021, that decreased to 45.59% of the overall vote with a majority in 122 of 213 municipalities.
The global marketing research firm Ipsos predicts that the party's support could fall as low as 30% in this election, resulting in an increase in coalition-run municipalities.
Naidu said the party had struggled to keep up with the expectations of evolving voters, particularly the Millennial and Gen Zdemographics, who now make up the bulk of voters.
"You have an electorate that wants to see who are these people that you're putting out there to say you're going to make things work for us," Naidu said.
Mbandazayo is one such voter. She is casting a ballot in her second election and said she was looking for a new voice in politics.
"We need change," Mbandazayo said. "I am considering voting for another party because the current party is not doing well for us because we've been voting for them for a long time."
South Africa has seen a wave of protests around migration for several months, ramping up in October with opposition to the country's asylum process.
According to Murmur Intelligence, a digital analysis firm, parties such as Action SA, the MK Party and the Patriotic Alliance have used immigration as a campaign issue.
"The party that might claim the most benefit from that sentiment … is Action SA," Murmur Intelligence co-founder Aldu Cornelissen said.

"They would make a clear argument that we need to get rid of illegal immigrants. We need to improve immigration. We need to protect our borders, which are all legitimate concerns, right? So, if any of the parties could capitalize on this sentiment, it would be them."
"But for what percentage?" Cornelissen said. "I would wager between 6% and 8%, roughly."
Those margins may seem low, but, in an increasingly fractured political landscape, parties are fighting for every vote.

According to the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC), 136,760 candidates are contesting across the country, with 75 parties contesting in Johannesburg, 70 in Tshwane and 69 in eThekwini (Durban and surrounding areas).

Fake news and false AI-generated content have become a feature in this election, with the IEC investigating more than 700 complaints of disinformation. One of the prominent claims has been an accusation that the ANC plans to mobilize asylum seekers to vote for them.
Asylum-seekers, refugees and permanent residents can't legally vote in South African elections regardless of how long they've been in the country.

William Bird, director of media monitoring agency Moxii Africa, said misinformation and disinformation "are now kind of part and parcel of your standard buildup to any electoral environment, wherever you are in the world."

"What we see with disinformation is that it always picks up on whatever the hot-button news issues are, as well as the standard kind of tropes about elections," he said. He added that there will always be "some bunch of clowns" saying the elections are rigged.

"And, in South Africa's case, there's no evidence to support that at all. The IEC is one of the best electoral-management bodies in the world. So of course, you then see people that are either wanting to destabilize, or they're wanting to just shake things up and make people scared or angry, and so they use those kinds of narratives. And that, unfortunately, is becoming an increasingly common trait," Bird told DW.
Bird said social media platforms often "incentivize and deliberately encourage people" to attack others online.

Municipal election turnout has historically been lower than turnout in national elections. In 2016, turnout was at 57.95% and dropped to 45.87%. In 2024, in the most recent national elections, turnout was at 58.64%.
Naidu said the election would ultimately depend less on online discussions or campaign slogans and more on how many people make it to the polls.
Voters will mark two ballots — one for a direct local representative and a second for a political party under a proportional representation (PR) system.
Seats allocated through the PR vote account for half of all council seats, making them as important as the direct votes for councilors and this is where voter turnout becomes a key element.

"That is why political parties are saying to people, go out and vote, go out and vote, because if you don't go out and vote, it has an impact on the calculation of what you win as a PR vote in the council and the seats that you get," she said. In turn, this affects the makeup of each municipality and whether new coalition governments will form.
Additional reporting by Ahmed Kajee and Sofia Christensen

articles.title: Greenland parliament approves security deal with US, Denmark

paras.en: Trump plans for ‘massive’ resource exploration in Greenland
Lawmakers in the semi-autonomous Danish territory of Greenland have approved an agreement with Denmark and the United States aimed at bolstering security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
The deal was passed 16-0 on Tuesday, with seven lawmakers abstaining.

The agreement was signed in September by US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
It followed months of negotiations behind the scenes amid growing tensions over Trump’s repeated threats to seize the vast, resource-rich Arctic island.
Greenlandic Foreign Minister Mute Egede said the ratification was another important step for the self-governing island.

“The road to this point has been a difficult one for us as a people. But we have stood firm on our fundamental principles, chosen dialogue and taken responsibility for our country’s interests,” he wrote in a post on Facebook.
“This is about all of us. The Greenland we love. About our security. And about our right to shape our own future,” he said.
Located between Europe and North America, Greenland is the world’s largest island, with a population of 57,000 people.
Trump’s refusal last year to rule out a military invasion had caused fear among Greenlanders, the majority of whom rejected US control, according to opinion polls.

The trilateral deal paves the way for more US bases on Greenland. It also allows the US to “modernise and expand” its activities at the Pituffik Space Base, a remote US military installation in northwest Greenland.
Under its terms, Greenland will remain under Danish control – but the agreement would still apply if the island eventually chooses independence.
The deal stipulates it will only “enter into force” once the “necessary parliamentary processes of the Kingdom of Denmark, in conjunction with Greenland, have been completed”.
Danish lawmakers are set to debate it later this month, while no approval is required from the US Senate.

articles.title: UK’s King Charles expresses ‘sorrow’ in Antigua over slave trade

paras.en: King Charles III has said at the official opening of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda that the transatlantic slave trade fills him with “horror” and “the most profound personal sorrow”.

The British monarch said on Tuesday that the slave trade “still casts a shadow over these [Caribbean] islands and other members of our Commonwealth”, and that the Royal Navy had played “a leading role” in ending it.
“We cannot change the actions of those who came before us,” Charles said. “We can, however, learn from the past.”
The king said he was seeking ways to address the wrongs by improving access to education, investing in jobs, encouraging trade among Commonwealth countries and pushing for climate resilience.
He ended the speech short of the apology that many Caribbean and African countries had hoped for. He offered no measures to address the economic and social damage of slavery.
Buckingham Palace had said the king would not issue a formal apology for slavery during his Caribbean tour, which also took him to the Bahamas and Guyana.
Guyanese President Mohamed Irfaan Ali said in an interview that an apology should be the king’s next step.
The dispute surfaced at the last Commonwealth summit in Samoa in 2024, when leaders called for discussions about reparations despite opposition from then-British Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
Last week, current British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK was open to a formal apology, while ruling out financial reparations.
Burnham, writing in The Guardian, said he wanted “to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people”.
He also proposed leading a programme of debt restructuring to help the Commonwealth’s poorest countries.
Ahead of Charles’s speech on Tuesday, a small group of protesters outside the venue held signs reading “Acknowledge the wrong. Commit to repair.”
“Technically, we’re free, but mentally a lot of us aren’t,” said Shana Michelle, from Antigua. “You have to apologise, yes. That is where we start with the repair.”
Leaders, including Burnham, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, were among those in attendance on Tuesday.
The Commonwealth has 56 member nations. Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne said, “No nation should be forced to mortgage its future simply to survive its present.”

articles.title: Yemen gov’t accuses IRGC, Hezbollah of sending 21 experts to back Houthis

paras.en: Yemen’s internationally recognised government has accused Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), as well as Lebanon’s Hezbollah, of deploying 21 experts to help the Houthis plan and direct military operations in the country.
Interior Minister Major-General Ibrahim Haidan said in a statement on Tuesday that 14 members of the group are from the IRGC and seven from Hezbollah.

The experts’ roles show that foreign involvement has moved from financing, arming and training to “direct supervision and participation in planning and managing operations and building military capabilities”, said Haidan.
The statement added that eight of the experts are in Hodeidah, four in Sanaa, four in Saada, two in Hajjah, two in Amran and one in the coastal city of Khokha.

It listed their specialities as including command and control, ballistic missiles and drones, electronic warfare, smuggling military components, coordinating naval operations and choosing commercial ships as targets, developing explosive-laden boats and autonomous submarines, and training fighters in mine-laying and siege tactics.
Haidan warned that the activities “threaten shipping in the Bab al-Mandeb strait and the Red Sea” and could transfer military expertise to other armed groups.

He called on the international community to designate the Houthis a “terrorist” organisation, dismantle their financing and arms networks, and enforce the arms embargo under United Nations Security Council resolutions 2216 and 2624.

The statement comes as Yemeni armed forces and fighters loyal to the government battle the Houthis in five provinces, after the group seized the western Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandeb area in September.
The resumption of fighting has shattered a relative quiet brought by a 2022 ceasefire that followed a lengthy civil war which first erupted in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa.
In 2015, Saudi Arabia entered the war at the head of an international coalition aimed at restoring Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

The government has long claimed the IRGC is supporting the Houthis, while Tehran insists the Houthis act independently. The Houthis acknowledge their alliance with Iran but have long denied being an Iranian proxy, while Hezbollah has previously rejected having a role in Yemen’s war.
Saudi Arabia, whose airports and oil facilities have come under Houthi attack in recent weeks, has accused Iran of encouraging the escalation.

Both parties are investing heavily in numerous House races. Republicans' closing message asked for two more years to fix issues, and Democrats argued they have already had too much time.

paras.en: by Jonaki Mehta, education correspondent focused on disabilities and learning differences

For half a century, America hasn't had enough special education teachers. It's a shortage that's only gotten worse as the number of students with disabilities grows rapidly — 8.2 million according to the most recent federal count, or about 1 in 6 students.

Research explains some of why these roles are so hard to fill: These teachers enjoy working with students but spend more time on legally required paperwork and tasks other than teaching. They often don't get paid more despite having more responsibilities than many other teachers. And because there's such a widespread shortage, the teachers who stay in the profession are often handed a bigger load.

NPR wanted to go beyond the research and hear directly from educators, so NPR senior producer Lauren Migaki and I have been exchanging voice memos with more than a dozen teachers from big and small districts around the country. So far, they've shared tales of joy when a student found success, tearful moments when they felt like they had failed, and waking up before dawn to make sure they were prepared.

For example, Jeffrey Carroll, who teaches in Newport News, Va., said last year, he was teaching students across three grade levels and multiple subjects: second, fourth and fifth. It meant he was constantly running from one classroom to the next. "I just didn't feel like I was teaching, I was never in a class long enough to be a meaningful part of it." This year, he was relieved to only be teaching across two grade levels. "It's been good to support my students in the classroom. I get to do some co-teaching. The lesson plans come to life."

articles.title: Indian navy rescues 20 crew from Iranian fishing boat hijacked off Somalia
articles.author: The Associated Press

paras.en: Indian navy rescues 20 crew from Iranian fishing boat hijacked off Somalia
MOGADISHU, Somalia — Indian naval forces freed an Iranian fishing boat and its crew of 20 hijacked off Somalia after an operation lasting more than 48 hours, India's Defense Ministry said Tuesday.
The rescue of the Azini was completed Monday in the Arabian Sea, more than 3,000 kilometers (1,865 miles) from Mumbai, Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said.

An official with the Puntland Maritime Police Force told The Associated Press that Indian forces disarmed 12 suspected Somali pirates, confiscated their mobile phones and released them. He spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the media.

The suspects and two Somali security guards later came ashore at Bandar Bayla in northeastern Somalia, the official said. Three of those who came ashore had minor injuries, but he did not specify whether they were suspects or guards, or how they were hurt.

India's ministry said the operation ended without casualties or injuries. It did not specify whether that account covered everyone aboard or only the rescued crew. It was unclear whether the crew remained on the vessel or were moved elsewhere.
The operation involved a warship, a maritime surveillance aircraft and marine commandos. An Indian Air Force C-17 aircraft airdropped additional commandos, the ministry said.

The Azini was hijacked Oct. 29 between Bandar Bayla and Hafun. A Puntland maritime police officer said on Sunday that it carried 21 Iranian crew members and two Somali security guards. The difference between that crew count and India's rescue figure could not immediately be explained.

Indian forces tracked the vessel by sea and air before securing it, the ministry said. It said there had been concern that pirates could use the boat as a floating base for attacks on commercial ships.
The Puntland official said regional authorities learned of the rescue only after it had taken place.

The hijacking followed a resurgence of Somali piracy across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean. By August, pirates had hijacked six commercial vessels since April, some far from Somalia's coast. They included the oil products tanker Sibu 1, seized about 252 kilometers (136 nautical miles) east of al-Mukalla, Yemen.

In September, Puntland authorities said pirates killed five crew members of the tanker MT Honour 25 before security forces recovered it. The tanker had been held since April. Authorities said they detained 16 suspected pirates.

The renewed piracy adds to shipping risks in a region already disrupted by the Iran war. Attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and threats by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi-linked shipping through Bab el-Mandeb have complicated oil transport routes.
Those disruptions have lengthened voyages and driven up tanker costs. Some oil shipments diverted around Africa face journeys up to a month longer.
International naval patrols and improved maritime security have sharply reduced Somali piracy over the past decade, but recent hijackings have renewed concerns about the threat.

articles.title: For Ukraine's Kherson region, a short ceasefire meant a momentary return to normal life
articles.author: Joanna Kakissis

paras.en: For Ukraine's Kherson region, a short ceasefire meant a momentary return to normal life
KHERSON, Ukraine — In this city where Russian drones usually fill the skies, Olena Soboleva could not easily walk down the street to meet her best friend, Anna Herasimenko.
Then came last week's truce, negotiated by First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, in a corner of southern Ukraine that included Kherson.
This weekend, the two friends, both 21, took the opportunity to venture outside to autumnal skies clear of drones and guided bombs.
"No drones, no explosions," Soboleva says. "No one wants to kill you."
They passed families strolling with their kids, shoppers stocking up on supplies and couples holding hands. They lined up at a cafe filled with paintings of cats.
"The city seems alive," says Herasimenko, "just like it used to be."
Over the weekend, she had also ventured to a salon.
"I did my nails," she says, showing off fresh burgundy polish. "The streets are full of people, just as they were in the past."

The truce ended Sunday night. Russia and Ukraine agreed to it in order to help Oleshky, a town across the Dnipro River from Kherson. Russian troops occupied Oleshky in 2022 and mined the land around it. Food and medicine rarely got through. NPR spoke to the families of residents there, who said their loved ones survived on pickles and boiled weeds.

Over the weekend, hundreds of Oleshky residents were evacuated, eventually escorted into northern Ukraine on buses. Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's ombudsman — the country's independent watchdog for human rights — thanked Melania Trump for ensuring that the ceasefire, which lasted from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1, happened.
"I believe they can be upheld and honored," Lubinets said about truces between Ukraine and Russia.

Even a short pause in hostilities was a respite for Kherson. Russian troops occupied the city for several months in 2022, until local partisans spied for Ukrainian soldiers, who then forced the Russians out of the city.

Since 2024, Russian troops based across the river have hunted Kherson residents with FPV (first-person-view) drones strapped with explosives. The highway into Kherson is shrouded in tunnels of heavy mesh nets to protect locals from these drones. These anti-drone nets also cover Kherson's streets and many of its buildings.
This weekend, cars pulled up next to the Greek-style monument marking the city's gateway.
Svitlana Vorobiova, a retired police officer, drove here from a safer city where she now lives. She took photos with her children at the monument.
"I have a place in Kherson, and my parents are also here," she says, and her voice breaks. Tears fill her eyes.
"I brought my son with me," Vorobiova says. "He hasn't been here in four years. He said, 'I cannot believe I'm in my hometown!'"

Inside the city, Volodymyr Mykolaienko, a former mayor of Kherson, strolls past the crushed remains of a once-grand administrative building. Locals stop him and shake his hand. He says he's happy to see so many people outside.
"I walk around the city a lot these days," he says. "I cannot sit still at home."

Mykolaienko, 66, spent years as a prisoner of war in Russia, confined to tiny rooms, starved and tortured. Russian troops arrested him in Kherson in early 2022, when the city was under Russian occupation. Mykolaienko was freed last year in a prisoner exchange and returned to Kherson, where his family still lives.
This truce allowed him to visit his father's grave. The cemetery is in a part of the city that's usually filled with drones.
"I could not hold myself back," he says. "I was able to do exactly what I have long wanted to do — to talk to my father, pray, thank him for my life and to tell him what was happening to our city."
At a busy bus stop, oncology nurse Olena Yehorova smiles at a gray-haired man playing folk music on his accordion.
"This truce has been such a relief," she says. "The people in our city have been able to breathe. Of course, we still walk around with caution, because you cannot trust the Russians."
She couldn't help looking up at the sky. A few hours later, the truce was over. She said she expects new attacks to resume at any time.
NPR's Polina Lytvynova contributed to this report from Kyiv.

This long intro APR is particularly handy for large balances (think anything $5,000+). The longer the promo window, the less you need to pay each month to clear your balance while paying no interest.

The Wells Fargo Reflect® Card charges no annual fee, so it costs nothing to keep in your wallet. For anyone building credit history -- or, like me, holding onto a top credit card for the long haul -- that's a real plus.
Keeping the card open can help your credit score by lengthening your average credit history over time.

The Wells Fargo Reflect® Card includes cellphone protection when you pay your monthly phone bill with the card. It covers up to $600 per claim for theft or damage, with a $25 deductible, and you can file up to two claims per 12-month period.
I've never had to use cellphone insurance, but as a frequent phone-dropper and generally clumsy person, I've always loved having it in my back pocket.
We recommend comparing options to ensure the card you're selecting is the best fit for you. To make your search easier, here's a short list of standout credit cards.
The Wells Fargo Reflect® Card earns no rewards. If you want a card with long-term perks like cash back or travel points, this isn't it.

A strong alternative is the Wells Fargo Active Cash® Card (rates and fees), which earns a flat 2% cash rewards on purchases for a $0 annual fee. It's our Best Overall Credit Card of 2026, and a fan favorite for flat-rate rewards.
The Wells Fargo Reflect® Card charges a balance transfer fee of 5%, min: $5 -- this is on the high side for a balance transfer card.
If you move a $10,000 balance, you'd owe a $500 fee, even though you'd pay the balance off at 0% during the intro period.

Run the math before you transfer, because the fee should cost less than the interest you'd otherwise pay. If you won't clear the balance within the 0% APR period, then an alternative balance transfer card with a lower transfer fee may serve you better.

The Wells Fargo Reflect® Card charges a 3% foreign transaction fee, so you'll pay extra on purchases made outside the U.S. If you travel abroad and want to skip that cost, consider one of our favorite travel credit cards.
It also has no purchase protection or extended warranty on purchases.

You'll generally need good to excellent credit (Motley Fool Money estimates this to be a FICO® Score of about 670 or higher) to qualify for the Wells Fargo Reflect® Card. Wells Fargo doesn't publish an official cutoff, and applicants closer to 700 tend to be the best-qualified candidates.

Keep in mind, your score isn't the only factor. Wells Fargo also weighs your income, existing debt, and overall credit history. You can check for pre-selected offers on Wells Fargo's site without a hard inquiry to gauge your chances first.

The Wells Fargo Reflect® Card comes with a minimum credit limit of $1,000, and higher scores and income generally earn higher limits. Wells Fargo sets your limit individually based on your full credit profile, so two applicants can get very different lines of credit.

Your starting limit isn't permanent, though. Once your account is open and in good standing, usually after six to 12 months, you can request an increase. Or, Wells Fargo may raise it automatically for on-time payments and low utilization.

To get the 0% intro APR for 21 months from account opening on qualifying balance transfers (then 17.74%, 24.24%, or 28.49% Variable APR), you must complete qualifying transfers within 120 days of opening your account.
I recommend starting the transfer online or by phone as soon as you're approved. Having your old account details ready speeds things up.
One important note: you can't transfer a balance from another Wells Fargo or affiliated card. Transfers have to come from a different issuer, and the 5%, min: $5 transfer fee applies to each one.

Approvals are usually instant, but can take a few days if Wells Fargo needs to verify some of your information.
Yes, the Wells Fargo Reflect® Card is worth it if your priority is paying off debt or financing a large purchase without interest. Very few cards give you a long no-interest runway like this.
It's not worth it if you want rewards or perks after the intro period, since it offers neither.
Ready to make a dent in your debt? Apply for the Wells Fargo Reflect® Card today -- awarded Motley Fool Money's Best 0% Intro APR Card of 2026.

When the 0% intro APR period ends, any remaining balance starts accruing interest at your regular variable APR from that point forward. The Wells Fargo Reflect® Card doesn't charge deferred or retroactive interest, so you only pay on what's left -- not on the full original balance.
